activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
Justin found the cuff in the kitchen drawer beside the takeout menus, a gift his father had ordered online and used exactly twice. The drawer still smelled faintly of the pharmacy aisle it had come from, that sterile plastic smell that his father called noxious and his mother called clean. His father was in the living room with his feet up, watching a game he did not seem to care about, and the pill bottle on the side table had his name on it in the pharmacist's careful block letters.

He had gone upstairs first, taking the steps two at a time, and by the time he sat on his bed his pulse was tapping in his throat. He slid his arm into the cuff, pressed the button, and watched the numbers climb. He wrote them down because Ms. Brennan had told them, back in the fall, that a measurement you did not record was a measurement you did not take. His father's doctor had said something at the appointment about numbers, and Justin had stood in the corner of the exam room nodding, understanding almost none of it.

The reading seemed high. He was almost sure it was high, though he could not have said what counted as normal, which was the whole problem. Ms. Brennan had assigned them a short talk on interpreting blood pressure and on how diet and exercise changed it, and Justin had put it off until the Sunday before, and now he was sitting on his bed with a machine and no idea what it was telling him.

He texted Layla, who was doing the same assignment and, by her own account, doing it better. She replied with a photograph of a pamphlet from the pharmacy on Miller Road, the kind of machine by the door where you sit and put your arm through a loop. She said her brother had used it once after sprinting for the bus and gotten a number that scared their mother, and then a calmer one later the same day. Justin read the text twice, then looked at his own scribbled number, then at the stairs he had just climbed.

He set the cuff aside and did nothing for a while. He made himself sit still, feet flat on the floor, because that felt like the opposite of what he had just done, and he rested his arm on the desk so that it sat roughly level with his heart, propped on a folded sweatshirt. He watched the second hand on his father's old alarm clock make five slow circuits. Then he ran the machine again.

The new number was noticeably lower than the first. He sat looking at the two figures side by side in his notebook, the same arm, the same machine, the same afternoon. The difference was not the cuff and it was not him, or not exactly him. It was the running up the stairs and the slouching and the arm held wrong, all of it folded into those first numbers like a lie told by a machine that could not lie.

He carried the notebook downstairs and read both numbers to his father, who paused the game. "So which one is real," his father asked, and Justin said, "The second one. You sit quiet about five minutes, feet flat, arm supported at heart level. Posture and activity change the numbers." His father looked at the cuff, then at the stairs, then at his son, and said he wished somebody had told him that when he bought the thing. Justin said he wished somebody had told him too.

They took his father's reading together, Justin arranging the chair, the sweatshirt, the arm, his father complaining the whole time in the particular grumbling way that meant he was grateful. Afterward Justin showed him the pamphlet photograph Layla had sent, the part about sodium and about walking, and his father said maybe they'd both start, and both of them heard the maybe for what it was. His father had been saying maybe about the stairs at the park since the diagnosis. Still, he ate the apple Justin handed him instead of the chips, which was something.

Justin thought about how the assignment kept asking him for a single true number, as if the body were a polity that could be counted once and governed accordingly. But the body was not like that. It answered differently depending on how you asked, and it seemed to him that the honest position was to hold both methods at once, the rushed one and the rested one, and to know which one you were looking at. What he could not settle was whether the first reading was a mistake or a kind of information too, a true account of his father under stress. He wrote that question in the margin and left it there.

On Monday he gave the talk with the two numbers from his notebook on the board, and Layla caught his eye from the second row when he described the five minutes and the flat feet and the supported arm, and nodded once. When he got to the part he did not know, the part about what the stressed number meant, he said so plainly, and the room went quiet in the way it does when someone stops performing. After class he checked his phone and found a message from his father, sent from the pharmacy on Miller Road: a photograph of the machine by the door, his father seated beside it with his sleeve rolled up, waiting.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
Gavin had told everyone, more than once, that the essay would be easy, that Ms. Malik's assignments were basically participation marks if you bothered to write in full sentences, and by Tuesday evening he had almost convinced himself that the reason he hadn't started was laziness rather than fear. The printout of the painting lay on the kitchen table between his laptop and a mug his mother had filled with tea he hadn't asked for and was already drinking. The painting was called The Broken Column, and the woman in it stood straight and split open down the middle, a stone column where her spine should have been, nails pushed into her skin, a landscape behind her cracked and dry.

Ms. Malik's instructions were taped above the desk in his room and copied into his notebook, three headings: colour, composition, symbolism. Formal analysis, she had said, meant describing what was actually there before deciding what it meant. Gavin had nodded at the time as though this were obvious. Now he wrote "the sky is grey-ish" and "she is crying" and read both back with contempt. Zachery, sprawled on the living room couch with his phone, had offered earlier to come over and help, and Gavin had said he didn't need help, which was not true, so when the doorbell rang at eight he felt relieved and slightly caught.

"You said you didn't need help," Zachery said, dropping his bag.

"I said I didn't need it. I can still accept it. Sit down."

They bent over the printout together. Zachery pointed at the strap around the woman's waist, the surgical corset, and said the white of it against her skin made her look like a broken statue being held together by a display case. Gavin wrote that down because it was better than anything he had, then felt the small sting of it and reminded himself that taking good ideas was also a skill, which was the kind of thing he told himself often and rarely believed. He argued instead that the vertical line of the column split the painting into two halves, the body and the landscape, so the composition made you compare them, one broken and one broken, mirror images.

"Okay, but why the nails," Zachery said. "That's symbolism. That's the part I'd fail."

Gavin opened his laptop to check whether the nails meant something specific, whether there was a code he was missing, some mythology of spikes. What he found first, on a museum page, was a date: September 17, 1925. He read the sentence twice. On that day, when Frida Kahlo was eighteen, a streetcar crashed into her bus, and the injuries caused her pain for the rest of her life. He did the arithmetic without meaning to. She was eighteen. He was sixteen, and he had spent the afternoon complaining to his mother that his shoulders hurt from carrying his laptop bag.

"She was basically my age," he said.

"Who was?"

"Kahlo. When the accident happened. The streetcar hit the bus she was on, and she was eighteen, and her whole body was basically wrecked from then on." He heard his own voice go flat, the way it did when he was absorbing something faster than he could shape it into an opinion. "She painted this almost twenty years later."

Zachery pulled the printout closer and was quiet in a way he usually wasn't. Gavin watched him look at the column in the woman's torso, and something in the painting rearranged itself without moving. The tears, which Gavin had dismissed as melodrama, now seemed almost restrained, two small drops, because a person who had hurt for that long would have learned that crying was not the interesting part. He typed: the symbolism is not exaggeration; it is inventory. Then he deleted it, because it sounded like something he'd stolen from a documentary, though the thought underneath it was his.

His mother came through with a plate of toast, having heard, Gavin suspected, the word accident from the kitchen and made her own quiet calculations about what they were looking at. She set it down without commentary, which was her way of noticing. On the phone earlier, Gavin's father had asked about the essay, and Gavin had told him it was going well, and had then nearly ruined the claim by pontificating for five minutes about composition until his father laughed and asked whether Ms. Malik was paying him an honorarium for the lecture. Ms. Malik, when Gavin had complained at school about the assignment's scope, had only said that he wrote incisive sentences when he stopped performing and started looking, and he had carried that home like a bruise he kept pressing.

He kept typing. He still didn't know, he admitted in the last paragraph he drafted that night, whether the grey sky meant grief or was simply the colour of the day she remembered, and he wrote that uncertainty down instead of hiding it, because pretending to know had been the thing Ms. Malik had caught him doing all semester. Zachery read over his shoulder and tapped the page once, at the line about her being eighteen, and said nothing, which between them meant it was the right line.

At eleven Gavin saved the draft, and the painting stayed open on the screen, the woman standing straight-backed in her field of cracks. His mother's mug, refilled, had gone cold beside the keyboard again.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
story:
The debate topic was taped to the whiteboard before anyone sat down: should the city charge more for water during a drought. Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no notes. Ms. Hernández said it once and then started taking attendance, as if she hadn't just rearranged the next three days of Ella's life.

Ella had chosen the side against higher charges because arguing felt easier when you could lean on being against something. What she hadn't counted on was the vocabulary. In her notebook she wrote lists of words she would need, escasez, impuesto, derecho, and read them under her breath while Malaika sharpened a pencil beside her with exaggerated calm.

"You're going to be fine," Malaika said. "You're better than Reese and he talks like he's already in college."

Reese wanted the other side and wanted it badly, which was the problem. He had family in a farming town where the wells had gone dry two summers ago, and he'd been reading about aquifers all week, sliding printouts across the table at lunch. He didn't just want to win. He wanted someone to understand what a profligate use of water looked like, lawns green in August, sprinklers hissing at noon, while his grandmother hauled buckets from a neighbor's tank. Ella knew this because he'd told her, twice, without being asked.

The practice round on Wednesday went wrong fast. Ella got through her opening sentence and then Reese stood up and said something rapid about infrastructure, and under the pressure her Spanish simply left. "That's not, okay, look, the point is," she said, and heard herself doing it again in the next breath, English flooding in where the other language should have been. Ms. Hernández didn't stop her. She just made a small mark in her book, which augured worse than any correction.

Afterward, in the hallway by the vending machines, Ella dropped her forehead against the cold metal. "I sound like an idiot. I keep mixing them."

Malaika unscrewed a bottle of juice. "My mom does that all day. At work, at home, halfway through a sentence. There's a word for it, code-switching. It's moving between two languages in one conversation." She shrugged. "She's not weak in either one. That's just what fluent people do."

"It's not allowed in the debate."

"So stop doing it, then. But stop thinking it means you're bad at this, because it doesn't." Malaika's older sister had a theory that half of senior year was convincing yourself of the wrong thing and then being miserable about it, and Malaika repeated this now, more or less, while feeding coins into the machine.

That night Ella tried something different. Instead of banning English, she let it in and translated on the spot, out loud, alone in the kitchen while her father watched television in the next room. When the English came she said the Spanish right after it, like a shadow, then again, then again, until the Spanish arrived first. The slips got shorter. They didn't vanish. She started to notice they came at the same moments, whenever Reese pushed on fairness, whenever the argument required her to say what she actually believed rather than what she could remember how to say.

The real debate, Friday, went like this. Ella opened with the drought, the reservoirs down, and argued that higher charges would fall hardest on the families who already used least, that a flat increase punished the wrong people. Reese answered with his grandmother's town, the green lawns of the city fifty miles away. Somewhere in the third minute he pushed hard on waste, and Ella felt the English rising in her, and instead of freezing she slowed down, took a breath, and found the sentence waiting in Spanish. Mostly. Twice a word escaped her, once she heard herself say "basically" in the middle of a clause, and she let it pass without flinching and kept going. Her position, when she reached it, was not the one she'd rehearsed. She said that Reese was right about waste, that some use of water was indefensible, and that charging more for basic use was still the wrong tool, that the two things could both be true. She wasn't sure the grammar held. She said it anyway.

At the five minute mark Ms. Hernández clicked her pen once and Reese exhaled through his teeth. He came over while Ella was stacking her notes, stood too close, and said, "The thing about the aquifer. You didn't answer that part."

"I know."

"So you're saying you don't know?"

Eella looked up at him. "I'm saying I don't know yet."

He stared at her for a second, then laughed, short and annoyed. "Fine. Monday. Same topic. My place, my grandmother's actually coming up, you can lose to her instead."

"Deal," Ella said, and shoved the notes into her bag before he could see her grin.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
story:
Naomi spread the two articles across the kitchen table like a dealer laying out cards, though she had no idea yet which one was the ace. Her mother set a mug of tea beside her without being asked, then went back to the sink, and that small unspoken kindness was the only part of the evening she felt sure about.

The assignment sheet said: compare two scholarly articles on the same question, evaluate their methods, arrive at a considered position. Ms. Kovalenko had been careful to say that "considered" did not mean "correct," and Naomi had written that word in her notebook and underlined it twice, because it seemed like the kind of thing that would matter later.

The first article, the older one, had a sheen of authority. It had been cited hundreds of times, its author celebrated in certain circles, almost lionized by people who believed he had been silenced rather than simply wrong. The second article was denser, duller, thick with tables, and had been cited thousands of times by people who seemed to find it boring in exactly the way trustworthy things are boring.

Vance had texted her an hour ago: still on for the library tomorrow? bring snacks. She had replied with a thumbs up and then felt guilty, because she hadn't told him what the articles were about. Vance's family didn't vaccinate. He'd mentioned it once, casually, a colloquialism about "big pharma" that he'd picked up from an uncle, and Naomi had let it pass because they were eating fries and the conversation had moved on to something easier.

She read the older article again, slower this time. Something snagged. She turned back a page, then forward, then back again, and got up to find a highlighter in the drawer by the phone, the drawer that held dead batteries and birthday candles and one glove.

The number was twelve. The older article, the one claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, was based on twelve children. Twelve. She sat with that for a moment, turning her mug in a slow circle on the tablecloth. Her cousin's wedding had a hundred and forty guests. Her chemistry class had twenty-six students. Twelve children, and a claim that had traveled around the world and back.

The second article was a study of hundreds of thousands of children. She didn't fully understand the statistics, the confidence intervals like fences around a number, but she understood scale. She understood that if you wanted to know something about all the children in the world, asking twelve of them was like tasting one spoonful of soup and reviewing the restaurant.

"Find something?" her mother asked, drying her hands.

"Sort of." Naomi tapped the page. "This famous paper, the one everybody argues about, it was twelve kids. The other one is like, half a million."

Her mother leaned over her shoulder. She smelled of dish soap and the garden. "Which one is the famous one?"

"This one. The twelve one."

Her mother was quiet in a way that changed the temperature of the room. "Your aunt sent me a video about that paper," she said. "Last spring."

Naomi looked up at her.

"I never finished it," her mother said. "The man was very convincing, the one in the video. He made it sound like the whole world had turned on him for being too altruistic." She pulled out the chair across from Naomi and sat down, which she almost never did at this hour, and folded her hands on the table. "Is it true? The twelve?"

"It's right here in the article. Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claimed the MMR vaccine caused autism, and the whole thing was twelve children." Naomi heard her own voice go flat with the size of it. "Twelve, Mom. That's it."

Her mother pulled the article toward her and read, moving her lips slightly, the way she did with anything official. Naomi watched her and thought about how easy it would have been to say something sharp, something about videos and uncles and spoonfuls of soup, and how none of that would help, and how the woman across the table had brought her tea without being asked.

"I liked the video," her mother said finally. "He seemed like he cared."

"Maybe he did." Naomi meant it, and was surprised that she did. "But the other study, the big one, the boring one. People made that too. Someone had to enter all that data. That's caring nobody makes a video about."

Her mother laughed, a short, real laugh, and pushed the article back across the table. "So what's your paper going to say?"

Naomi picked up her pen. "I don't know yet," she said, which was true. She knew which study she trusted, and she knew that trust wasn't the same as proof, and she knew there was a difference between explaining something to Ms. Kovalenko and explaining it to her aunt. The position she was building felt like a bridge she could only build from one end.

She texted Vance: bringing snacks and also I need to tell you what my paper is about, it's weird. Then she pulled a clean sheet of paper toward her and wrote, at the top, in handwriting she hoped looked steadier than she felt: "Twelve children, and everything after."

Her mother got up, refilled the kettle, and put it back on for a second cup.

story:
The library smelled of floor wax and old paper, and the radiator under the window ticked like something counting down. Katherine spread her notes across the table: fourteen index cards, every one of them in French, on the question of whether nuclear deterrence still made sense in Europe. In forty minutes she had to stand in front of Mr. Ivanova and debate the topic for five minutes without a word of English.

She had written it as an argument. Deterrence had prevented great-power war since 1945; the risks of proliferation were manageable; disarmament would destabilize regions where trust was already thin. She read the first card aloud under her breath, and the French came out flat, each clause landing with the same weight, like stones dropped one at a time into a well.

"You're rehearsing to nobody," said Louis-Philippe, dropping into the chair opposite her with a thermos and his usual nonchalant slouch, as if the deadline were someone else's problem. He was doing the same assignment; their teacher had paired them as opponents. "You sound like a vending machine."

"At least I sound like something."

He leaned over and flipped through her cards without asking. "Every card is a fact. Numbers, treaties, one footnote about Kant. Where are you in this?"

"Kant is not a fact, he's an argument," she said, but she knew what he meant. She took the cards back and squared them, and the gesture reminded her of her grandmother, who used to square her own cards before bridge, and that reminded her of something older. In eighth grade she had watched a debate where a boy argued brilliantly for something everyone already believed, and the room had nodded along until a girl on the other side stood up and said only one sentence: "You've never been the one waiting for the bus that didn't come." The room had shifted. Katherine had never understood, until now, what the girl had actually done.

She pulled the textbook Mr. Ivanova had left on the reserve shelf, the one with the cracked spine, and turned to the chapter on rhetoric. There it was, in a paragraph she must have read and forgotten: Aristotle had named three means of persuasion. Ethos was the speaker's credibility. Pathos was the audience's emotions. Logos was the logic of the argument.

"Everything I have is logos," she said. She laid the cards out in a fan. "All three of these are logos. This one's still logos."

"So add the other two," Louis-Philippe said, unscrewing his thermos. The smell of coffee mixed with the wax and paper. "Easier in French?"

"Nothing is easier in French."

She tried anyway. Ethos, she decided, was not a card; it was the way she stood, the moments she admitted uncertainty instead of pretending the numbers settled everything. Her grandmother used to say that people trusted you fastest when you told them what you didn't know. Katherine wrote on a fresh card, in French: "I do not claim the risks are small. I claim they are smaller than the alternative." Her handwriting wobbled on the last word because the bell above the study room door had just rung, and Mr. Ivanova was early.

He sat down with a legal pad and a timer. "Louis-Philippe, you first, or Katherine?"

"Her," Louis-Philippe said, and had the decency to look slightly ashamed of it.

She stood. The study room was small and too warm, and the window behind Mr. Ivanova showed the parking lot, where a groundskeeper was pushing a wheelbarrow of sand toward the salt shed. Katherine began with her strongest card, the logic, and heard again the flat stones dropping into the well. Then she set the card face down on the table, which was not in any of her plans, and said, in French, that she had grown up eleven kilometres from a base she had only learned about last year, and that she did not know whether that made her safer or simply closer.

Mr. Ivanova stopped writing. Louis-Philippe put down his thermos.

She kept going. The five minutes held a strange shape: logic for two, then the admission, then back to the argument about destabilization, but now the room was listening differently, leaning in rather than sitting back. When the timer sounded she was mid-sentence on a point she no longer remembered making a case for, something about how deterrence was a promise whose credibility depended on being willing to keep it, which was a thought she had not had before she said it aloud.

"Ferme," Mr. Ivanova said, and made a note. "Again Thursday. Louis-Philippe, you're up, and you should worry, because she just used pathos and you have forty index cards of statistics."

Katherine sat down and gathered her fan of cards, all logos, and the one new card with the wobbly handwriting. Louis-Philippe was already shuffling his own deck with the look of someone who understood, for the first time all week, that he was behind. Outside, the groundskeeper tipped the sand into the shed and stood for a moment with his hands empty.

"How do I get the grandmother thing in French?" he asked.

"You don't," Katherine said. "You have to have a grandmother thing first."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
story:
Noemie had claimed the corner table at the coffee shop an hour ago, and her laptop still showed the same paragraph, rewritten eleven times. Across the rim of her cup, Natalie was texting with both thumbs, and Curtis was folding a napkin into smaller and smaller squares, which he did when he was working up to something.

"You're writing it wrong," Curtis said finally. He said it to the napkin first, then to Noemie.

"Thanks. Very detailed feedback."

"I mean the format. The whole thing." He pulled out his phone, scrolled, and turned the screen toward her. It was an email from his cousin, forwarded twice, and beneath it a page from the admissions service. "Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, they got rid of the free-form personal statement. It's three structured questions now. Why you want the subject, and how you've prepared. Three questions, fixed, not one big essay."

Noemie looked at her screen. Six weeks of drafting. A opening anecdote about her grandmother's greenhouse that she had polished until it shone and meant nothing. The waiting had been enervating her for days, that specific drained heaviness of doing nothing while everything hung open, and now it turned out she had been drained over the wrong document entirely.

"I wrote the old one," Natalie said, not looking up from her phone. "Last month. Four hundred words about how chemistry found me." She did look up then. "Is that bad?"

"It's not bad," Noemie said, and heard how unconvincing it sounded. "It's salvageable. Probably."

Curtis, who had read the whole page twice, said the cousin had told him the opposite thing at Christmas, that the personal statement was where you made them love you, and he'd believed it, and had been planning to copy the cousin's structure line for line. The cousin had applied years ago, when the form was one open essay and a person could be charming on paper. Curtis said this with the flat voice he used for things that embarrassed him.

In the spring, Noemie remembered, Ms. Whitaker had stopped her after class and asked what she was writing about. "Why medicine," Noemie had told her, and Ms. Whitaker had nodded and said, "Keep evidence of that," and Noemie had assumed it was one of those things teachers said, the way her father said to check the tyres before a long drive. She had not asked what Ms. Whitaker meant. She had gone home and worked on the greenhouse anecdote instead.

Natalie watched Noemie read the three questions for the second time, then a third. She had known Noemie since they were eleven, and she knew the stillness that came over her before she either gave up or got angry or, occasionally, got interested. This looked like the third one. "You're not even upset," Natalie said.

"I'm reallocating." Noemie opened a new document. Her cursor blinked in the empty top left corner. The greenhouse story could become a paragraph under the second question, why she'd prepared, how she'd spent two summers measuring soil chemistry for a neighbour who paid her in tomatoes and a reference letter. The first question, why medicine, was harder, because the honest answer involved her grandfather's last winter, and honesty like that either worked or it didn't, and there was no way to know from this side of the decision.

Behind the counter, the espresso machine screamed and went quiet. At the next table, a man was telling someone about his pension, about turning his savings into an annuity, payments for life, guaranteed, and Noemie found herself listening to the word with something like envy. Annuity, certainty paid out on a schedule. An admissions decision was the opposite, a door that opened once on a date she could not control.

"Order up," the barista called, and Curtis collected the drinks because Noemie was typing now, fast, the greenhouse paragraph cut and pasted and trimmed, and Natalie said, "Wait, you're helping me with mine after," and Noemie said, "After," and did not look up.

The bell over the door rang, and Ms. Whitaker came in, shaking rain off her coat, and stopped when she saw the three of them crowded around one laptop, three faces lit by a single screen. She came over slowly, reading the page upside down, and put her hand briefly on the back of Noemie's chair.

"You found it," Ms. Whitaker said.

"You knew," Noemie said. "In the spring. You told me to keep evidence."

"I did know." Ms. Whitaker pulled out the empty chair and sat down uninvited. "I also knew that if I handed you the change, you'd treat it as another instruction, like the word count. Another box." She nodded at the screen. "I wanted to see what you'd do when the box wasn't the one you expected."

Natalie broke the silence first. "So is my chemistry-found-me essay a total loss?"

"Open a new document," Noemie said, and turned the laptop so Natalie could see. "Question two. Start with the summer programme. And you," to Ms. Whitaker, "are buying the coffee."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
The keys were heavier than Ethan expected, or maybe he only imagined that, the way he imagined his father's silence in the passenger seat would be worse than yelling. His father had insisted on the empty church lot first, then, without announcement, pointed at the road out of town, and now Ethan was doing forty on County Nine with his hands at ten and two and his father's coffee cup sweating in the holder between them.

"Watch your speed," his father said. Not a yell. Worse, in a way, the flat calm of a man bracing for something.

Ethan eased off the gas. He had passed his written test two weeks ago, perfect on the signs, one wrong on right-of-way, and Josie had teased him about it in the parking lot after school, saying the permit was the state's way of letting you denigrate yourself legally, behind the wheel, at fifteen miles an hour, in front of witnesses. He had laughed then. He did not laugh now. Ahead, the road split into two lanes feeding the highway ramp, and a sign the size of a dinner plate said MERGE LEFT.

"Signal," his father said.

He signaled. He checked the mirror. The left lane was clear, silver and empty all the way back to the water tower, and he began to turn the wheel.

His father's hand came across his chest, not grabbing, just there, a bar of knuckles and old watch. "Stop. Look over your shoulder first."

Ethan froze, wheel half-turned, and turned his head. A blue hatchback sat in the left lane beside them, close enough that he could see the driver's elbow out the window, could see the thumbnail chip in her windshield. He had not seen it in the mirror at all. It had simply not been there, and then it was, and his heart was going like something small trapped in a wall.

"That's your blind spot," his father said. "Mirror can't cover it. You have to turn your head."

They merged after the hatchback passed, the driver giving them a long look Ethan could feel on the side of his face. His father sipped his coffee. The interstate unrolled ahead, and Ethan held the lane and thought, with a strange clarity, about the way his father drove every day, head flicking left and right like a bird's, and how Ethan had always assumed it was nervousness, a tic, something to be endured on long trips. It was arithmetic. Every driver ran a rolling bordered country they could not fully see, and the head-turn was the tax you paid to live in it.

"Josie failed her first road test," Ethan said, to fill the silence, to hear his own voice do something other than apologize. "She didn't check her blind spot either. She told me the examiner grabbed the wheel and she failed in the first ninety seconds. She's retaking it Tuesday."

"Good friend to have," his father said. "Someone who tells you the failure before you live it." There was something almost warm in it, and also something obdurate, his father holding his position on the coffee cup, refusing to say the near miss had been nothing, refusing to say it had been everything.

Ethan thought of the two pictures of driving he carried: the one from the movies, all ease and one-handed confidence, and the one his driving manual laid out in its dense stratum of rules, each paragraph another layer pressed down over the last, all of it built on the simple fact that the seat hides parts of the world. He had preferred the first picture. He suspected the second was truer, but he could not yet feel it in his hands, and he was honest enough with himself to know that. Maybe by the time he drove Josie to her retest, if she passed and he got his license, it would be both things at once. Maybe it never settled.

"Exit's in a mile," his father said. "You'll want the right lane."

Ethan signaled. He looked in the mirror, and the mirror showed him nothing but road, so he did not trust it. He turned his head, shoulder rotating against the seatbelt, into the small wedge of world the car had been hiding from him, and it was empty this time, and he moved over anyway, slow, like a man checking a dark room.

The banners were already up in the gym, and the seniors had been herded into the main hallway for the third rehearsal of the week, lining up alphabetically while a student council member with a clipboard tried to make the process seem orderly. Peyton stood between Bree and Annabella, holding the speech she had drafted and rewritten four times, the pages soft at the corners from handling. She was supposed to deliver it at commencement on Saturday, two minutes maximum, an injunction Ms. Rivera had issued with the flat certainty of someone who had endured a dozen student speeches about following your dreams. Peyton's problem was simpler and harder: she no longer believed a word of what she had written.

"It's a pageant," she said to Bree as the line began to shuffle forward. "We walk in a circle to the same music every school in the country plays, someone reads our names wrong, and everyone pretends it means something. Then we're done."

Bree adjusted her cap, which she had decorated with tiny painted stars despite the rule against decorating caps. "You're allowed to think it's a pageant and still walk in it. Those aren't opposites."

"They kind of are." Peyton flipped to her speech, the paragraph about embracing the future with courage and integrity, and felt her jaundiced view of the whole enterprise harden into something like anger. "I can't stand up there and say this. I'd be pontificating in a polyester gown."

From where Annabella stood, two rows ahead and half-listening, it looked like Peyton was about to tear the pages in half, and Annabella reached back and grabbed her friend's sleeve just as Ms. Rivera moved down the line checking names against her clipboard. "Save the crisis for after the rehearsal," Annabella whispered, and Peyton, embarrassed, stuffed the speech into her gown's pocket instead.

That evening, avoiding the speech, she opened her Othello text for the last time, planning to return it to Ms. Rivera's classroom shelf before graduation cleared out her locker. She was skimming the third act, half her mind on the ceremony she resented, when the phrase surfaced on the page and stopped her: the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. She read it twice. She had walked across stages to that music since fifth grade, had heard the band saw through it every June, and it had never once occurred to her that the tune had words behind it, let alone those words. A quick search on her phone confirmed what the play was already telling her: Elgar had taken the title Pomp and Circumstance from this line in Othello. The march that she had dismissed as empty pageantry was named after a line about the hollow glory of war.

She sat with that for a while, the textbook open on her desk, the speech crumpled beside it. If the music itself carried that irony, then maybe the ceremony had never been pretending to be pure. Maybe everyone marching knew, somewhere underneath, that the ritual was borrowed and slightly absurd, and walked anyway, because walking together was still worth doing. That was not the same as believing the polyester pageant was sacred. It was closer to holding both ideas at once and admitting she could not fully reconcile them. She picked up a pen and started a new draft, not about courage and integrity, but about a march whose name came from a tragedy, and about choosing to walk it regardless.

At the final rehearsal on Friday, she found Ms. Rivera by the gym doors. "I rewrote it," Peyton said. "It's still under two minutes. But it's honest now, or closer to honest. I might read part of Othello."

Ms. Rivera looked at her for a moment over the clipboard. "You're the one who argued with me about the seating chart in October. I should have guessed you'd argue with the ceremony itself." She made a small mark on her list. "Read the Othello. But if you tell them what to think about it, I'm cutting you off at the two minutes."

"I wasn't going to tell them what to think," Peyton said. "I don't totally know what I think."

On Saturday morning the hallway outside the gym smelled like hot polyester and corsages, and the line formed itself the way water finds a channel, without anyone directing it. Bree's starred cap glinted under the fluorescents. Somewhere ahead, the band began the opening chords, and Peyton felt the familiar swell of the music she had resented all week. She still did not know whether the march meant anything, or whether meaning was something the march could carry at all. But her new speech was folded in her pocket, and the phrase from the play was running through her head, and when the line moved forward, she stepped with it. Annabella, glancing back, caught her eye and mouthed, ready, and Peyton nodded, and walked through the doors into the noise and the light.

story:
The computer lab at Camp Winowish smelled of pine through the open screens and of burnt coffee from the counselor's station, and Jason had claimed the corner terminal on the first day for a reason he hadn't admitted to anyone: from there he could see both the whiteboard and the lake, and he liked knowing that the lake was still going about its business while he failed at something indoors. His project for the final week was a Book class in Java, private fields, getter methods, a test to prove it all worked, and by Thursday afternoon he had the fields hidden away like money under a floorboard and the getters returning exactly what they were given.

"That's it," Terrence said, leaning over Jason's shoulder with the confidence of someone who had finished his own project two days early and regretted it ever since. "Add the constructor and you're golden."

The trouble began with Elliot, who had been quiet all week, turning his chair in slow arcs the way he did when a problem had him cornered. "My test died," Elliot said. He said it lightly, the way you report weather, but his hands had gone still on the keyboard. "It worked yesterday. I added a constructor with parameters this morning and now the old line won't compile. It's like the door I was using just isn't there anymore."

Jason rolled his chair over. On Elliot's screen sat a call that created a Book with no arguments, the way it had worked all week, and beneath it the compiler's flat refusal. Elliot had written the class with no constructor at all, at first, and the test had run anyway; that much Jason remembered clearly, because he'd been a little offended at the time that Java would do work for you that you hadn't done yourself.

"Wait," Jason said. He pulled up his own files side by side, his test and Elliot's, and ran his fingers along the edge of the table. "Before today, neither of us wrote a constructor. And it compiled. So something was making one for us." He looked at the error again, then at his own screen, where his constructor with parameters sat half-finished and his old no-argument test waited below it like a guest who hadn't heard the party was over. He wrote it out on the whiteboard in green marker, the two situations, and beneath them the sentence he was slowly daring to believe: if a class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default no-argument one, but once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added. "Default," he said aloud, tapping the word. "That's what it's called. A default no-argument constructor."

"So I broke my own code by improving it," Elliot said. There was something almost relieved in his voice, the way people sound when a mystery turns out to have a shape. Ms. Santos, who taught the afternoon session and had drifted over without commenting, raised her eyebrows at Jason and said nothing, which from her was a kind of applause.

Jason sat back down and, out of a loyalty he didn't examine too closely, typed a second constructor into his own class, one with no arguments, so his old test would run again beside the new one. It felt like keeping a promise to a past version of himself, that kid on Monday who hadn't known what private meant and had trusted the compiler to be generous forever. In a way, the whole week had been an argument about trust: Terrence wanted everything explicit, every field guarded, every door labeled, while Elliot wrote code the way you tell a story to a friend, assuming the listener would fill in what was missing. Jason had spent five days suspecting one of them was right, and now he thought the truth was more boring and more interesting than that: the compiler was generous exactly until you asked it to be something else, and after that, every kindness had to be built by hand.

At dinner Terrence stood up mid-meal and eulogized the default constructor, one hand on his heart, "It served this cabin faithfully and asked for nothing," while Elliot laughed so hard he knocked over his juice and Ms. Santos slid her napkin across the table before Elliot even asked. Later, out on the dock, the three of them argued about whether the compiler's change of behavior was a betrayal or just causality, Jason holding that it was neither, that a rule you never read was still a rule, and Terrence calling the whole idea of hidden defaults obsolescent, the kind of convenience that would be gone from the language in ten years. Elliot said the lake made it hard to stay angry at a compiler, and nobody argued with that.

They stayed until the bugs started, and then Jason said he wanted to try one more thing before lights-out. In the lab, alone with the corner terminal and the window gone dark, he deleted his no-argument constructor on purpose, watched the old test fail the way Elliot's had, and then wrote it back in, letter by letter, like a man learning a name he intended to keep.

story:
Rachel counted the boxes in the hallway of her new building twice, as if counting might reduce them. Eleven. The elevator smelled of cabbage and floor polish. From the fourth-floor window she could see the bus loop at the end of the street, a gray circle of asphalt with a shelter whose plastic had gone jaundiced from sun, and she decided, standing there with her duffel still on her shoulder, that she hated it. Not the building, not the town, just that loop, as though it had been built specifically to remind her that Milan and Alessio were two hundred miles away and had not yet answered the group chat.

She rode the bus the first morning because her mother said walking forty minutes in the rain was stubbornness, not principle. The route made eleven stops before the school, each one a name she could not yet connect to a face or a shop. She sat with her forehead against the glass and drafted a message to Milan: You would hate this. You would make fun of every single stop. She deleted it before sending, because it wasn't true, probably. Milan made fun of things and then liked them. That was Milan's whole method.

Ms. Visser lived across the landing, 4C, and watered a row of geraniums in the corridor window as though the corridor were a garden that owed her rent. On the fourth evening she caught Rachel struggling with a mattress pad in the stairwell and held the door without comment, which Rachel appreciated more than any speech about how the town would grow on her. Two girls from 4F had already given her a speech like that. Rachel had smiled with her teeth together and said nothing.

Alessio wrote back before Milan did. The message came while she was unpacking a box of books she had no shelf for, and she sat on the floor of the half-empty room to read it. They lost the semifinal. Coach put Dev in at the end, you can guess how that went. Also I'm taking psych senior year, we just did this thing, Zajonc, 1968. It's called the mere-exposure effect. People like things more just because they've seen them more often. Teacher showed us these faces. Anyway. Do you have a window.

She typed back that she had two windows and a bus loop, and that the bus loop was proof against his psychology, because she had now seen it fourteen times and hated it more each time. Alessio replied with a single question mark. She put the phone face-down on the cardboard and did not pick it up again that night.

But by the end of the month something had shifted without her permission. She noticed it on a Tuesday, standing at the shelter in the thin light, when the bus rounded the loop and she felt the small loosening in her chest that she used to feel at the corner by Milan's old house. She tested it, deliberately, the way you press a bruise. Hated stop, the mattress store. Hated stop, the church with the crooked sign. Then she looked down the aisle at the driver, at the woman with the folding cart, at the boy from her English class, and understood that she had been running the experiment on herself every morning, eleven exposures a day, and that the results were coming in whether she consented or not. It did not feel like a maxim or a rule. It felt like weather.

She was honest enough to hold the other idea too, the one Alessio's message had not settled. Liking something because it was familiar was not the same as choosing it, and she could not tell yet which of the two she was doing, or whether the difference would matter by June. When Ms. Visver, Ms. Visser, knocked that evening to say the water would be off until nine, Rachel found herself saying, almost beseeching, "Can I ask you something? Did you like this building when you moved in?" Ms. Visser considered the geraniums for a moment and said, "I don't remember liking it. I remember being here." Then she went back across the landing and closed her door, and Rachel stood in her own doorway with that sentence, turning it over like a coin she couldn't read in the dark.

On Friday she wrote to Milan at last, a real message, not a joke with a hole in it. I'm starting to like the bus route, she typed. I don't know if that means anything. She was still deciding whether to add more when Milan's reply came through, faster than any message he had sent all month. Funny you say that. There's a new girl in my calc class, sits in your old seat. I didn't like her at first. Rachel read it twice, then looked up at the sound of the bus grinding around the loop below, its headlights sweeping her ceiling.

story:
Hayden set the recipe on the counter and turned the oven dial to 190, the way his mother always did, palm flat over the knobs as if she were swearing an oath. She was working the late shift, and he had promised her a proper dinner, not pasta from a box. Carbonara, the recipe said, which sounded impressive and turned out to be bacon, eggs, cheese and spaghetti, four ingredients pretending to be a restaurant. His father sat in the living room with his bad knee up, shouting corrections at a football match, and Hayden could hear his little sister's cartoon from the other side of the wall. He put the bacon on to fry because that seemed like the first thing, and the smell of it filled the kitchen with something almost like a Sunday.

He was halfway through, spaghetti in the pot, bacon crisping, when he opened the fridge and stood there with the door's cold on his face. No eggs. The shelf held butter, half an onion in cling film, three yogurts, and a jar of something that had turned bellicose, its lid straining, its contents clearly plotting something. The recipe needed three eggs, and it needed them off the heat, beaten and ready, in about four minutes. He checked the door of the fridge, where eggs always lived at his grandmother's house, and found only hot sauce and a receipt.

He texted Emmy first because she cooked, actually cooked, the way other people played guitar. There are no eggs, he wrote, and I'm already halfway through. Help. Then he stood over the bacon with the spatula and did not move it, watching the fat spit, and the whole dinner balanced in his mind like a plate on a stick.

His phone buzzed. "Mise en place," Emmy wrote, and then, before he could ask: "It's French. It means putting in place. You measure and prepare everything before you start to cook." Then a second message: "That's why cooks set everything out first." He read it twice while the bacon told him, in its own language, that it was about to burn.

He remembered then his grandmother's kitchen, the summer he was eleven, the year his parents were separating and he was sent to her for July. She used to line up little bowls along her counter before she made anything, each one holding exactly what it held: a measured pile of flour, a small pool of oil, eggs sitting together in one bowl like a clutch of stones. He had thought it was some old-person ritual, the same woman who ironed tea towels, and he had asked her once why she didn't just get things as she went. She had shrugged and said, in her flat, unbothered way, that a cook who is hunting for things while the pan is hot is a cook who is already behind. He had not understood it then. He understood it now, with a pan behind him and no eggs anywhere.

He pulled the bacon off and texted Emmy that the neighbour, Mr. Nkosi, might have eggs. He had met him twice, once when a ball went over the fence and once when Mr. Nkosi returned their bin from the middle of the road without mentioning whose fault that was. He looked like a man who kept eggs.

The door took a long time to open. Mr. Nkosi was in a dressing gown with a crossword folded under one arm, and Hayden stood on the step feeling the full stupidity of the request. "Sir, this is going to sound ridiculous, but do you have three eggs? I'm cooking dinner and I did it wrong."

Mr. Nkosi looked at him for a moment, and Hayden braced himself for a lecture on planning, but instead the man said, "Four," and turned back inside. When he returned he held a bowl with four eggs in it and the crossword still under his arm. "One is for the road," he said, "in case you crack one badly." Hayden said thank you twice, and Mr. Nkosi waved it off, and then, just as Hayden was stepping down, added: "A fry-up man myself. Eggs are always in place in my house." He said it lightly, but Hayden caught it, the way the words lined up with Emmy's texts, and he walked back across the gardens grinning at the ground.

Back in the kitchen he beat the eggs with the cheese and plenty of black pepper, and pulled the spaghetti off a minute early because Emmy's recipe said the pasta should finish in the pan. His sister wandered in, drawn by the smell, and he set her on a stool with the job of grating more cheese, which she did unevenly and with enormous pride. His father hobbled in near the end, saw the pans, saw the bowl of sauce waiting, and went quiet in the way he went quiet when something surprised him. "Your mum's going to think we ordered this," he said, and Hayden said, "She won't, because the eggs came from next door and I'll have to tell her." He mixed everything off the heat, the eggs turning to a glossy sauce instead of scrambled bits, and even he could see it had worked.

They ate at the table because he insisted, and his sister told the story of the eggs in a voice that made Mr. Nkosi sound like a wizard. When his mother came home and found the pan soaking and a plate covered in foil for her, she stood in the doorway a moment before she sat down. He told her about mise en place while she ate, about Emmy's texts and his grandmother's little bowls, and how he had thought of it while the bacon burned almost, and how the whole thing felt like a line you keep approaching but never quite reach, some ideal of being ready that no one actually gets to. "You still got dinner on the table," his mother said, mouth full. "The asymptote fed us, then."

The next morning he found a plastic container on the step with a slice of the carbonara in it and a note in small, careful capitals: FOR THE EGG MAN. His sister had gone over the fence before him. Hayden took the container next door anyway, to knock, to say it again properly, and Mr. Nkosi opened up holding a fork, already eating.

story:
Gabriella had claimed the small table on her grandmother's screened porch as her own by the second morning of the visit, spreading her laptop, a battered notebook, and a mug of coffee that had gone cold an hour earlier. The summer camp's final project was due Sunday: build a Java class called Song with private fields and getter methods, then test it. She had written classes before, plenty of them, always the same way, class first, fields, constructors, then a quick test at the end to prove the thing ran. What she hadn't done was what the instructor's note at the bottom of the assignment suggested, almost as a dare: try writing the test before the class exists.

"That's backwards," her grandmother said, setting down a plate of peach slices. She had been a seamstress for forty years and regarded all computer work with polite suspicion. "You don't cut the pattern after you sew the dress."

"That's what I said," Gabriella told her. "But the guy who made it popular, Kent Beck, apparently designed it that way on purpose." She'd found it the night before, buried in a forum thread: test-driven development, a cycle of red, green, refactor. Write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code. She understood the words individually and the whole not at all, which was a sensation she disliked the way one dislikes a pebble in a shoe.

Noemy had texted her twice that morning. did you start?? and then, i did the class first like always, took twenty minutes, done. Gabriella looked at the message, then at her blank SongTest.java file, and felt the small hierarchy of summer camp settle over her, the people who finished first and the people who didn't. Susan was probably done too. Susan had finished the last project while everyone else was still reading the prompt.

She wrote the test anyway. It felt absurd, like dictating a letter to someone who didn't exist yet. The test demanded a Song constructor that took a title and an artist, and it called getTitle and getArtist and checked what came back. When she ran it, the compiler refused the whole file; Song wasn't a class, so there was nothing to construct, nothing to get. The console showed a bar of hard red. "Okay," she said to the porch, to the wrens, to the fan turning slowly overhead. "That's the red part, I guess. Failing test first."

Then she built the class. Private fields, a constructor, two getters, nothing more, because the test only asked for that much. When she ran it again the bar went green and something in her chest went quietly green too. But the assignment wanted a third field, length in seconds, and here her two habits collided. Her old self wanted to write the whole class at once, every field she could imagine, getLength, setLength, a toString, a display method for good measure, all of it bulking the file like a defense against future assignments. The test-first way wanted her to write one more failing test and let the class grow only as far as the evidence demanded. One way treated the class as a finished thing she was transcribing; the other treated it as something evanescent, arriving only at the moment a test called for it, never a line sooner.

She sat with that for a while, eating peaches. Mr. Esposito, the neighbor who came every Thursday to check the grandmother's gutters, waved at her through the screen. "Still doing the computer," he said, not quite a question.

"Trying to decide what a song is," she said.

"Depends on who's listening," he said, and went back to his ladder.

It was a joke, but it landed oddly. Her two approaches weren't just about order of typing; they were two little ontologies, two answers to what a Song fundamentally was. Was it a container defined by everything it might ever hold, or a thing defined only by what someone could prove they needed? She thought of Noemy's twenty minutes, the finished class heavy with unused methods, and of her own half-built one, lean, all of it accounted for. She couldn't fully convince herself that either was right. The big-class way prepared for futures that usually came; the test-first way refused to guess. Maybe it depended on the future, which was exactly the thing you couldn't consult.

She wrote the test for length. Red. She added the field and getter. Green. Then, on the third step, she understood what refactor was for: her constructor now took three parameters in a tangled order she'd chosen half asleep, and the test made the tangle visible, made it safe to fix, because if she broke something the bar would go red again and tell her. She cleaned it, ran the tests, watched them stay green. Her grandmother came out with iced tea and stood behind her chair for a moment, watching the screen the way she watched weather.

"Did you sew the dress before the pattern after all?" Gabriella asked.

"Cut a little, sew a little, cut a little more," her grandmother said. "That's how anything gets made right. The pattern isn't the dress." She set down the glass and went in to answer the phone.

Gabriella texted Noemy: you were right that the class was easy. but there's a third part after green, you clean it up, and I kind of like who I am during it. Then, worrying that sounded like more than she meant, she deleted the second half and sent only the first sentence. She ran the tests once more anyway, all green, and screenshotted the bar to keep, though she knew by tonight it would seem like a small thing, one assignment among the many that would metastasize into a whole degree, a whole adulthood. Noemy replied with a single thumbs up. Susan, copying the thread's instructor, wrote: red green refactor, Kent Beck. Gabriella smiled at the porch, closed the laptop halfway, and ate the last peach slice off the plate.

story:
The two textbooks lay open on either side of the keyboard, and Jack had been staring at them for ten minutes without typing anything. The school's book, the one Mr. Owusu had assigned, said the causes of the First World War were shared among the great powers, a tangle of alliances and mobilization schedules. The older book, the one his father had used at the same school twenty years ago and had dug out of the garage that morning, said Germany had wanted it. The differences weren't cosmetic. One said shared blame, one said German guilt, and the essay due Friday demanded a position.

He typed "who caused world war one germany textbook" and scrolled past the homework-helper sites. Somewhere in the third page of results a phrase kept recurring, attached to a name: Fischer controversy. He clicked.

Fischer. Fritz Fischer, a German historian. In his 1961 book, Griff nach der Weltmacht, he had argued that Imperial Germany had deliberately pursued a world war, and the claim had set off a long debate, the one the results kept calling the Fischer controversy. Jack read that sentence three times. A German historian, arguing that his own country had wanted the war, in 1961, when plenty of people who had lived through it were still alive to be furious. He opened a second tab, then a third, and the debate unrolled: other historians attacking Fischer, defending him, revising him, each with documents the others hadn't weighed or had weighed differently.

The front door slammed. Haydn came into the kitchen dropping his bag, and found Jack still at the screen an hour later. "You've been on that all afternoon?"

"Look." Jack turned the laptop. "The books disagree because the historians disagree. There was this guy, Fischer. Sixty-one, Griff nach der Weltmacht, and he said Germany went after a world war on purpose. That's the Fischer controversy. It's been going ever since."

"So which one's right?"

"That's what I'm trying to figure out."

"You're going to fail the essay figuring." Haydn pulled up a chair anyway, because Haydn could never leave a question alone either.

Jack showed him the counter-arguments, the replies to the replies. Alek arrived at six with the math homework neither of them had started, saw the screen, and immediately took the other side, because Alek always took the other side. "Fischer had documents," Alek said. "Documents are documents."

"Fischer had some documents," Jack said. "The other guys had different ones. They're all looking at pieces."

"That's so weak," Alek said. "You can't write 'everyone's sort of right.'"

Mr. Owusu lived three doors down, and Jack had promised his mother he'd return the spare ladder before dark, so he carried it over with the laptop tucked under his arm, planning to ask one question on the doorstep. Mr. Owusu listened with the ladder already in his hand and didn't lecture. He only said, "Whose voices survived the archive, Jack? And whose didn't?" Then he carried the ladder into the garage and left Jack standing on the walk with the question getting heavier the longer he held it.

Back home, alone at the screen, Jack understood what he'd been circling. The historians weren't failing to find the answer; they were asking different questions of what remained, and what remained was partial. An epistemology classmate of his sister's had once described, at dinner, as the study of how you know anything at all. His father's textbook wasn't wrong so much as older, written when the questions were different, when the argument hadn't yet forced every textbook to take a side. Jack began to type, slowly at first, then faster: the war's causes as a contested field, Fischer's claim laid out with its opponents, and his own position, held open where the sources ran out. It was the first essay he'd written where he admitted, in the last paragraph, what he could not settle.

He didn't try to sublimate the frustration of that admission into some tidy conclusion, either. He let it sit on the page. He printed the essay at eleven, stapled it, and set it by his keys.

At school on Monday, Mr. Owusu handed the essays back with a single comment in red at the bottom of Jack's: "Excellent. But which textbook did you use?" Jack looked down at his bibliography, and realized he'd cited only his father's book, the old one, the one that said Germany did it. He'd spent the whole weekend defending uncertainty, using the one source that agreed with what he'd wanted to believe in the first place.

"The new one's in my locker," he said.

"Bring both next time," Mr. Owusu said, and moved on down the row.

The night before Eid, the cultural center smelled of cardamom and floor polish, and Clara's mother stood at the donation table with an envelope of cash, counting on her fingers for the third time. "Six," she said. "Your grandmother, me, you, Auntie Rusul, Uncle Karim, Layla." She pushed the envelope toward Mr. Dela Cruz, who ran the center's office and had stayed late to collect the charity, and Clara, stacking folding chairs against the wall, heard her own name go into the count like a coin.

She had helped prepare for the celebration all week, draping string lights along the stage where the Eid prayer would happen at sunrise, taping paper lanterns that Zachariah had cut crooked and insisted were "abstract." She liked the work. What she had never done was think about the money. So when Mr. Dela Cruz began writing receipts, she came over and asked what the envelope was for, and her mother said, "Zakat al-fitr," the way she said all the Arabic words, quick and unbothered, as if the name settled everything.

It didn't settle everything. Clara watched Mr. Dela Cruz count out the amount, the same amount for every family, multiplied by the number of people in it. "It has to reach the poor before the Eid prayer," he said, mostly to the receipt book, "so that they can celebrate too." That was all. Nobody delivered a lecture. But Clara stood there feeling the shape of it: the charity was timed like a threshold, a door everyone was meant to walk through at the same moment, nobody kept waiting outside while the feast began.

She went back to the chairs, but the count followed her. Six people, six shares, and one of the six was her. Her mother was Muslim; her father was not; they had divorced when she was nine, and for years Clara had been an amalgam of two households, fasting some Ramadans and decorating Christmas trees with an enthusiasm she used to cover her confusion. Seventeen now, she still couldn't say what she believed. She believed in the feeling of the prayer hall at sunrise. She believed in her grandmother's hands cupped over her face. Beyond that the ground got soft.

Zachariah found her in the kitchen, where she was pouring tea from the big dented pot, and he could tell from her face that she was somewhere else. He was mercurial that way, bouncing from jokes to seriousness without warning, and now he skipped the jokes entirely. "You look like you failed a quiz." She hadn't failed anything. She told him about the six shares, about her own name in the count, and then, because he was already pouring himself tea like he owned the kitchen, she told him the part she hadn't said out loud to anyone: that she didn't know if she counted.

"Counted as what?" Zachariah said. "Muslim enough? Who's doing the math on that?" He meant it lightly, but he waited for a real answer, and Clara found she didn't have one. Her mother would say of course she counted; she was her daughter, she fasted the hard days, she was at the center on a Thursday night stacking chairs. Her father, if asked, would say believing mattered more than belonging, and Clara suspected both of them were partly right, which was the most inconvenient possible position.

In the morning she arrived early, before the prayer, while the light through the high windows transfixed the whole hall, catching dust and the sequins on little girls' dresses so that the room seemed to hold still. The donation table had moved outside under the awning, and a line had formed, families arriving with their envelopes, the charity due before the prayer began. Clara's mother was near the front with her grandmother and Auntie Rusul. Clara hung back, then walked to the table, took out the twenty she had brought from her weekend job at the bakery, and set it beside the receipt book. "For me," she said to Mr. Dela Cruz. "A seventh. From me, for me."

He wrote it without comment, which she understood was a kind of respect. She took her place in the row with her family, shoulder to shoulder with strangers, and when the imam's voice rose she did not close her eyes. She kept them open, watching the light shift across the floor, thinking of the envelope already gone, delivered somewhere across town so that another table would have food on it today. She still could not have said what she believed. But when her grandmother reached over and pressed Clara's hand flat against the carpet, as if pinning it there, Clara let it stay.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
story:
The room still smelled like the lemon cleaner the janitor used on Fridays, and Zoey sat in the third row of Ms. Wilson's empty classroom during lunch, refreshing the college portal on her phone even though she knew nothing posted until at least five o'clock. She had taken the SAT in March, the digital version, and for three weeks afterward she had been certain she had ruined it. The second math module had been brutal, the kind of questions with three stacked equations and answer choices that all looked plausible, and she had guessed on the last four.

Cristina came in eating a bag of chips and dropped into the desk beside her, upside down, facing backward. "You're doing the refresh thing again."

"I'm doing the refresh thing," Zoey agreed. She set the phone face down on the desk like evidence at a trial she was losing.

Melanie arrived a minute later with two milks and slid one across to Zoey without being asked, which was the kind of thing that made Zoey's throat tight lately, small kindnesses landing harder than they should. "Ms. Wilson said you could eat in here as long as we don't get crumbs near the Chromebooks," Melanie said. "She was scathing about the crumbs, actually."

"Ms. Wilson is scathing about everything," Cristina said. "Remember when Marcus left a banana peel on the radiator."

Zoey didn't laugh. She turned the phone over again, then over once more, a coin with no heads. "I keep thinking about the second module," she said. "It was so hard. Way harder than the practice tests. And I just, I keep replaying it, all the ones I guessed on."

Melanie set down her milk. "Okay, wait. Do you know how the digital one works?" She leaned forward, elbows on the desk. "It's adaptive. The test switched to that format in March, in the States. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second one."

Zoey stared at her. "Sets the difficulty."

"If you did well on the first math module, the second one gets harder," Melanie said. "A hard second module might mean you earned it. You did well on the first one, so it gave you the harder questions."

Cristina crumpled the chip bag slowly, watching Zoey's face change. "So all that panicking you did for three weeks," she said, "was maybe because you did well?"

"Maybe," Zoey said, but the word had a different weight than it had carried all morning. She thought about how she had walked out of the test center certain of failure, how she had told her mother not to expect much, how she had drafted a whole essay in her head about applying to the state school as a fallback, a way to codify her disappointment into a plan so it would hurt less when it arrived. She had built a whole structure on a guess she hadn't known she was misreading.

Ms. Wilson came back in for her coffee mug and paused at the door. "Scores?" she asked, not unkindly.

"Not till five," Zoey said.

"They'll be what they'll be," Ms. Wilson said, and left with her mug, and somehow that was the most useful thing an adult had said to her all month.

The three of them sat with it. Melanie drew a little adaptive tree on the corner of Zoey's notes page, first module branching into an easier path and a harder path, and Zoey looked at it and thought about how the test had made a judgment about her, in real time, silently, without anything that resembled a mind or what her philosophy homework called sentience, and yet it had changed her whole evening, her whole three weeks, her whole sense of what she deserved. A machine had looked at her first twenty-two answers and decided she was worth challenging, and she had read that challenge as punishment.

"It's not proof," she said out loud, testing it. "Hard module could still mean I bombed both. I could have done well on the first one and then choked on the hard second one anyway."

"True," Melanie said.

"So I know less than I thought I did before you told me, but also more," Zoey said. "That's a horrible place to be."

"It's the honest place," Cristina said, and stole one of Zoey's fries from the bag she hadn't opened yet, which didn't make sense, and neither of them mentioned it.

At 4:52 they were still there, Ms. Wilson grading at her desk and pretending not to watch, the March light going long and orange across the whiteboard. Zoey held the phone in both hands. She understood now that whatever number appeared, she would read it through two stories at once: the story where the hard module was a reward, and the story where it was a wall she'd hit at full speed. She could not make them into one story yet. Maybe she never would, maybe that was fine, maybe the admissions office would decide for her and she would spend a year believing whichever version hurt less.

At 5:01 the screen changed. She saw the word first, before the number, the word that said whether the March test had been kind to her, and Melanie grabbed her arm, and Cristina stood up so fast her chair scraped, and Zoey read it, and read it again.

"Go on," Cristina said. "Tell us."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
story:
Victoria had spread the two articles across her grandmother's dining table, which was normally reserved for holidays and which her grandmother had ceded to her for the week with the words, "Do what you like with it, just don't lose my coasters." The first article claimed that listening to music while studying improved recall, and it reported three experiments, all of them significant. The second article, by a different team using a different method, found the same thing. So did the third and fourth she'd printed at the library before the drive out here. Ms. Hoang had assigned a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and had said the interesting papers would be the ones where the writer took a side, or refused to. Victoria had underlined "or refused to" twice.

The problem was that taking a side felt impossible when the sides agreed. Every study she found supported the effect. She sat at the table with a legal pad, wrote "why is everything the same," and then felt embarrassed and crossed it out.

Her grandfather came through with a mug of tea he hadn't been asked for and set it on a coaster. He read upside down, slowly, the way he read everything. "All these say the same thing," he said.

"That's the point," Victoria said. "That's how you know it's true."

He made a sound that could have meant anything and went back to the kitchen. He had worked his whole life in quality control at a plant that made bolts, and he did not believe in uniformity the way other people did.

She texted Jude, who was doing the same assignment with articles on growth mindset, and asked whether he'd found anything that didn't work. "no," he wrote back, "why would i go looking for stuff that doesn't work." She didn't have an answer, but the question sat wrong with her, the way a level sitting wrong on a shelf sits wrong. She opened her laptop again on the sunporch, where the afternoon light made the screen hard to read, and started searching in the other direction: studies of music and memory that found no effect, or a negative effect, or nothing at all.

They were hard to find, but not because they didn't exist. She found one, in a middling journal, with a small sample and a null result. She found a conference poster, never followed by a paper. She found a doctoral dissertation that ended with the sentence "these findings did not support the hypothesis," and then nothing, no citation trail, as though the thing had walked into a field and lain down. Leo, who was on the same group chat, sent a link an hour later with the caption "found the word for what you're doing." It was a short piece by a psychologist named Robert Rosenthal, from 1979, and it had a name for what she'd noticed.

"The file drawer problem," she said out loud to the empty sunporch. Studies with null results went unpublished, sitting in drawers, which made the published record look more positive than the evidence actually was. She read the sentence three times. The tea had gone cold on the dining table by then, and the two articles she was supposed to be reviewing looked different to her now, less like two witnesses agreeing and more like two survivors of the same filter.

That shift made the writing harder, not easier. She drafted a paragraph arguing that the agreement between the two articles was itself the thing to analyze, then scrapped it because it sounded like she was dodging Ms. Hoang's demand for a position. She drafted a second version saying the evidence supported the effect, and hated it, because she now knew she could only say the published evidence supported it. The distinction felt small and enormous at once. Her grandmother came out to the sunporch to deadhead the geraniums and asked how the paper was going, and Victoria said, "I don't know who to believe," and her grandmother said, "Start with who's telling you," and went inside before Victoria could decide whether that was advice or just something a person says.

She called a kind of truce with the assignment, a detente between her two drafts. The review would say that the two articles, read side by side, were convincing, and that she could not tell how convincing, because she could see the drawer but not into it. She wrote a paragraph on what a reader would need in order to settle it, and then, because it was honest, a shorter paragraph on what she could not know from where she sat. The old rotary phone on the hallway table rang while she typed, an anachronistic sound her grandparents kept around on purpose, and she heard her grandfather answer it in the kitchen, saying nothing for a long time the way he did, as if the silence on the line were a finding worth recording.

At dinner she explained the file drawer problem to her grandfather over his silent objections, then Jude by text, then Leo, who replied "wait so the absence of stuff is evidence." She typed back that she wasn't sure absence could be evidence if you couldn't count it, and he sent back a shrug emoji, and she put the phone face down and cut into her potatoes. Near the end of the meal her grandfather said, "At the plant, when a bolt failed the test, we wrote it down. The bolt didn't go in the drawer."

"Studies aren't bolts," Victoria said.

"No," he said. He picked up his fork. "The people are the same, though."

She went back to the table after the dishes and reread her last paragraph, the one about what stayed uncertain. Then she opened a blank page, typed a single question at the top, and left it there for the morning.
