activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
story:
The video arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, in the group chat with Elliot and Kalen, captioned only with a fire emoji and the words "our river." In it, a stretch of brown water surged over a parking lot, shoving a blue kayak against a chain-link fence while a man's voice offscreen kept saying holy, holy. Below, Elliot had typed: share this everywhere, they're hiding it.

Leo had already typed a reply, something like "insane," when he stopped himself. He could remember, though he rarely said so, the time in tenth grade when he had forwarded a story about a school closing and half his grade had stayed home on a false alarm. The embarrassment had not faded so much as metastasized into a private rule: check before you send. But he had never actually learned how to check anything. He knew the rule and not the method, which, he was beginning to understand, left the rule mostly decorative.

He biked to Kalen's house the next afternoon because Kalen had a desk, two monitors, and the patience of someone who read terms of service for entertainment. "So I want to see if this flood video is real," Leo said, "before I send it to like forty people." Kalen pulled the clip up and then, almost immediately, hit a wall that seemed to embarrass them both: Leo suggested reverse-searching the video itself, and the image engines just shrugged, returning nothing usable. "You can't just search a video," Kalen said, spinning his pen. "Most of these engines don't take it."

For a minute they sat there, two boys defeated by a search bar. Then Kalen stopped the clip on the frame with the kayak pinned against the fence, took a screenshot, cropped it, and dropped the image into the search bar. That worked. The engine returned a wall of thumbnails, and fourth from the left was the same kayak, same fence, same brown water. The date under it was from three years ago. Leo leaned closer. The top result came from a regional news site, a town two provinces away, and the caption mentioned a spring flood, a burst culvert, ancillary road damage, and a volunteer cleanup that had raised money for, of all things, a kayak club. None of it was their river. None of it was now.

"So it's real," Kalen said slowly, "but it's not ours." That was the part Leo hadn't expected to feel like a problem. A fake video would have been simple; he could have told Elliot it was fabricated and felt righteous. Instead the clip was honest footage wearing a lie as a caption, and the lie was the kind people wanted to believe, the kind that suggested something was being hidden from them. Leo remembered the false school closing again, how the correction had travelled at a tenth of the speed of the rumor, and how the kids who had stayed home had mostly shrugged and gone back to bed.

They kept pulling screenshots: the fence, the parking lot, a shot of the man's shoes at the edge of the frame. Each image search returned fragments of the same 2019 coverage. Leo took out his phone and started a reply in the group chat, then deleted it, then started it again, then deleted that. Telling Elliot felt like accusing him, and not telling him felt like watching him walk into traffic. He drafted something neutral: "reverse-searched some frames, it's from a different flood, 2019." Then he sat on it.

Ms. Chen, Kalen's mother, knocked and brought in cut apples, and paused at the screen long enough to recognize the news site. "That outlet's decent," she said. "They retract things when they're wrong, which is more than I can say for most people I know." She said it lightly, but Leo heard the secondary meaning, the small fiduciary weight of trust placed in an outlet that earned it, and he thought about the forty people in his own contact list who had placed something like that in him without ever saying so.

He finally sent the message. The reply came fast, three dots, then: "yeah I know." Then: "check the account that posted it." Leo opened the original post. The account had been created that month, had no other posts, and followed exactly one person. He tapped through to that one follower and stopped, because the profile picture was a photo he himself had taken, at Elliot's birthday, of Elliot's dog. Below the dog, the name field read, in lowercase, "a project for media class."

The doorbell rang, and it was Elliot, holding his phone up like a hall pass, already grinning, already talking about grades and whether Leo had checked the fence or the shoes first. "Which frame got you," Elliot said, dropping onto the bed. Leo looked at the screenshot still frozen on the monitor, the kayak pressed against the wire, and said, "The fence. Show me how you cropped out the date."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
The bell over the door of Mr. Malik's bookshop had a small crack in it, so it rang twice, once cleanly and once sourly, and Sebastian had come to judge his entrance by which note came first. Today the sour one. He carried the paperback in his jacket, spine already soft from a week of reading on the bus, and found Cloe at the back table where the shop kept its kettle and its mismatched chairs, three books open in front of her and a look of deliberate calm.

"You didn't do the response," he said.

"I did something better." She slid a sheet across the table. At the top she had written, in her narrow hand, a passage copied out from Jane Eyre, the part where Jane tells Rochester she is not talking to him through the medium of custom, conventionalities, nor even of mortal flesh. Below it, two columns. One said: what a Marxist sees. The other said: what a feminist sees. The columns were half empty. "Mr. Malik said if we can't argue both sides we can't argue either. I think he made that up, but it sounded true."

Sebastian sat down without taking off his jacket. He had spent four days trying to get the passage to mean one clean thing, and every time he thought he had it, the other lens came and undid his work. Through the Marxist lens Jane was a governess, an employee, her passion a rebellion against wage labour itself, her plainness a fact of her purse. Through the feminist lens the same sentences burned with something else, a woman claiming an equal soul in a world that had never once asked whether she had one. He had written and discarded three drafts. His want was simple and slightly shameful: he wanted to be right in front of Cloe, who was never wrong and never gloated about it, which was worse.

"That column's empty," he said, pointing at the feminist one.

"It's not empty. It's waiting." She turned the sheet around. "I found something in my grandmother's attic last weekend. Come on."

Behind the counter, among the books Mr. Malik priced but never shelved, Cloe had set an old volume, cloth-bound, its cover rubbed to the colour of dried grass. She opened it to the title page with both hands, the way you handle something older than your grandparents. Sebastian leaned in.

Jane Eyre. An Autobiography. Edited by Currer Bell. He read the line twice. London, 1847. "Who's Currer Bell?"

"That's the thing. Currer Bell was Charlotte Brontë. She first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, and the name doesn't tell you the author was a woman."

Sebastian straightened up. Something rearranged itself in his head, quietly, the way furniture moves in a dark room. "So the first readers didn't know."

"The first reviewers thought they were reading a man. Some of them liked it better once they suspected otherwise, and some liked it worse."

Mr. Malik came around the counter with two mugs and set them down without ceremony. He had opinions about people who hovered over his books with hot tea, and he had given them these mugs anyway, which was his way of joining a conversation without having one. "Don't spill," he said, and went back to the till, where a customer was trying to decide between two paperback biographies and clearly wanted to be talked out of one.

Sebastian pulled the sheet toward him and began to write in the empty column, slowly at first. If the book had to arrive wearing a man's name, then Jane's speech to Rochester, her refusal to pass through the medium of custom, was not only a scene in the novel; it was the novel's whole situation, speaking from inside a disguise. And the Marxist column was not cancelled by this. He kept both. A governess with no property speaking as an equal to a man who owns the house she works in, and the woman who invented her needing a false name to be read at all. The two readings sat side by side, overlapping, and he could not make them one thing, and he wrote that down too, in the margin, where Mr. Malik would see he had at least been honest.

"Look at you," Cloe said, but softly.

"It doesn't settle anything."

"I know. That's why I left the column half empty. I wanted somebody to fill it wrong first so I could fix it." She took her pen and, instead of fixing, added a question mark after half his sentences.

Outside, the light was going amber over the street, and a bus went past with an advertisement for some noxious energy drink peeling off its flank. Sebastian thought of how he had almost not come tonight, had almost stayed home with his three dead drafts and the sour idea that not deciding was the same as failing. He sipped the tea, which was too strong and probably deliberate.

Mr. Malik called from the till, not looking up. "You two. When you're finished arguing with the Victorians, there's a shelf of Russians back there that will do you good. Whole novels like a steppe. Nothing happens for a hundred pages and then everything does."

Cloe closed the old volume along the line of its worn hinge, careful as folding a map. "Can we come back Sunday?"

"Shop opens at ten," Mr. Malik said, and rang up the biography the customer hadn't wanted.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
Natalie had the keys in her fist before Ms. Ma even reached the driveway, which Ms. Ma noted aloud with a raised eyebrow, saying that enthusiasm was fine but the handbrake came first. The car was her mother's, a manual, a squat grey hatchback that had carried Natalie to eleven years of school runs and now sat in the evening light looking smaller than she remembered. Ms. Ma, who had taught half the street to drive and took payment in either cash or, once, a fully repaired gutter, lowered herself into the passenger seat and set her coffee in the cup holder with the gravity of a judge placing a gavel.

"Clutch down, start her up," Ms. Ma said. Natalie pressed the wrong pedal, and the engine made no complaint at all, which somehow felt worse than a complaint. "That one. Left. It's the skinny one, like the pedal is on a diet." Natalie found it, and the engine caught, and the whole car trembled around her like something waking up.

The first half hour was a study in small failures. She stalled at the end of the driveway, twice, and Jayden, who was washing his own car three houses down with the slow diligence of someone avoiding homework, called out, "Third time's the charm," and she stuck her arm out the window and gave him a thumbs up she did not feel. Ms. Ma talked her through the biting point, the little rise in the revs, the shudder in the seat, and on the fourth attempt the car rolled forward up the road, smooth as anything, and Natalie laughed, a startled bark of a laugh, because she had not expected moving to feel that easy.

They came back and parked, and Natalie sat with her hands on the wheel, sweating in a way she felt was unbecoming, and Ms. Ma drank her coffee. Then Jayden wandered over, drying his hands on his shorts, and asked why she was bothering with manual at all. His instructor had an automatic, he said. Automatics were the future. Nobody in London needed gears. He was going to be driving within a month, effortlessly, while she was still stalling at junctions like a Victorian motorist.

"That's true," Natalie said, and she meant it, and this was the thing she had been chewing on all week. Automatic was easier. Automatic was, in a way, fairer, because it removed a barrier that had nothing to do with whether you could actually judge traffic or distance or rain. She had half decided to switch to automatic lessons, and had even rung a school about it, and the woman on the phone had been very kind and very clear. In the UK, if you pass your test in an automatic, you can drive only automatics. To drive a manual, you have to pass a manual test. Full stop. Jayden's licence would be a smaller licence, and he did not seem to know it.

"It's true," she said again, gentler this time, because Jayden looked genuinely wounded, the way people do when a plan is contradicted. "Pass in an automatic and that's all you're licensed for. You'd have to do another test for a manual." He argued for a minute, then got his phone out, then went quiet, then said, "Well, that's stupid," in the tone of someone who has lost an argument to a webpage. Ms. Ma, impervious to the whole debate, was watching a cat cross the road with an air of professional interest.

But Jayden's point did not die just because the rule existed, and Natalie knew it. There was a version of her that agreed with him, that thought difficulty for its own sake was an ideologue's game, that a good system should remove pointless friction rather than enshrine it. Her mother's car, though, was not an argument. It was a car. It sat in the driveway needing a driver, and her mother's knees were worse this year, and on Thursdays someone had to get to the supermarket and back. The principle of ease could not underwrite a Thursday. Practicality, on the other hand, had no answer for the question of whether she would stall at the first roundabout and shame herself before a busload of strangers. Both things were true. She held them the way you hold two bags of shopping, one in each hand, and did not put either down.

"I'm sticking with manual," she said. "Not because it's noble. Because of Thursdays." Jayden said Thursdays were a low bar for a life philosophy, and Ms. Ma said that in forty years of teaching, Thursdays had motivated more people than philosophy ever had.

"Right," said Ms. Ma, and drained her coffee, and pointed her chin at the road where the cat had been. "Once more up the street, and this time you're going to change into second, and if you grind the gears I want you to know it's normal and I will still flinch." Natalie pressed the clutch, found the biting point, and pulled out past Jayden, who was waving the towel like a flag.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
The book arrived on Tuesday, three weeks late, and Brooke lugged it up to her room before anyone could ask why a girl who had sworn off the library still owed it twenty dollars in fines. The paper was due Friday. She had her argument, sort of, something about how reform movements get remembered, but she had no footnotes, no bibliography, and a style guide open on her laptop like a foreign phrasebook.

Her mother called up that the pasta would be ready in twenty minutes, and Brooke said "okay" twice, the second time to herself, because the book she'd ordered used was filled with someone else's notes. Down one page, the footnotes marched in a pattern she'd never seen: a full citation, then a line that read only "Ibid.", then another "Ibid., 44." She turned the book sideways as if that might help. "What are you," she said to the page.

She texted Maisie. Do you know what Ibid means. Maisie replied with a shrugging emoji and the words "sounds like a disease," which made Brooke laugh, and then, because Maisie was two streets over and bored, there were footsteps on the stairs a few minutes later, Maisie holding a jar of instant coffee like a peace offering.

"Show me the disease," Maisie said, dropping onto the bed.

Brooke opened to the page. "There. It just says Ibid. Three times. Is the author lazy or is this a code?"

Maisie squinted at it. "Maybe it's Latin. Everything terrible is Latin."

They looked it up on Brooke's laptop, Maisie's chin almost on her shoulder, the way they used to read over each other's shoulders in middle school. "It abbreviates ibidem," Brooke read, "'in the same place.' You use it when your note cites the same source as the note just before it." She sat back. "So the author isn't lazy. He's being precise. It's a way of saying, again, the same book, here."

"So it's not a disease."

"It's a courtesy. Like knocking before you cite."

Maisie spooned coffee into two mugs of hot water and declared it undrinkable, then drank it anyway. "Your paper's about why people romanticize the past, right? You could use that. Someone writes a whole book about one argument and then just says ibid, ibid, ibid, trusting you to remember where you are."

Brooke had been thinking something adjacent to that, though she hadn't found the words yet. Her draft argued that nostalgia was a real political force, not just sentiment, and Mr. Sun had written in the margin of her proposal, "Careful. Don't pathologize your opponents; describe them." She'd been annoyed at the time, feeling that calling a movement reactionary was simply accurate, but now she wondered whether accuracy and dismissal could share a sentence. She pulled the laptop toward her and started typing while Maisie narrated the pasta smell from downstairs.

"You're going to write the whole thing tonight?"

"I'm going to write the argument tonight. The footnotes I'll do tomorrow, which is a petulant thing to do to my future self, but she'll cope."

At dinner Brooke ate fast and went back up, and by eleven she had a thesis she actually half believed: that the movements she was studying weren't lying about the past so much as selecting from it, and that a critic's job was to show the selection without pretending the feeling behind it was sickness. She wasn't sure it held. She was sure it was arguable, which Mr. Sun said was the actual assignment.

The footnotes took longer than the writing. At one in the morning she cited the same source twice in a row and typed, experimentally, "Ibid." It looked naked there, trusting a reader to look up. She deleted it and wrote the citation out in full, then put "Ibid." back, then deleted it again. There was something in the choice she couldn't name: whether precision meant repeating yourself or assuming the reader could follow. She left it in, finally, and made tea she didn't drink.

Friday morning Mr. Sun returned the papers at the end of class, and as the bell rang he paused at Brooke's desk, tapping her third page with one finger.

"Ibid.," he said. "Old school. Did you know what it meant before Tuesday?"

"Before Tuesday I thought it was a diagnosis."

He laughed and gathered his folders. Brooke slid the paper into her bag unread, saving the grade for the walk home, where the late book sat on her desk with its borrowed footnotes, and she photographed the strangest one, the fourth ibid down, and sent it to Maisie with no caption at all.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
story:
The kettle had been on for ten minutes before Sophia noticed it, and by then the kitchen window was fogged so completely that her grandmother's garden had disappeared. She was sitting at the table with her chemistry workbook open to a page she had avoided for three days, the one about equilibrium, and beside her the kettle ticked as it cooled, patient as a cat. Her grandmother was upstairs resting her hip, and the house held that particular quiet of late afternoon, clemency after a week of heat that had cracked the municipal water restrictions and yellowed the lawn.

The problem was simple to state. A reaction at equilibrium, in a sealed container; the temperature rises; which way does the equilibrium shift? Sophia had copied the equation onto scrap paper twice, and twice it had sat there doing nothing for her. She understood concentration changes, understood pressure, because those could be pictured, gas crowding toward one side or another like students funnelling through a doorway. Temperature refused to picture itself. It was everywhere in the problem and nowhere in the equation.

Her phone buzzed on the table. Carla, from the study group she'd skipped to come out here: did you get the temp ones? Sophia typed that she was still working on them, then set the phone face down, because Carla's messages had a way of arriving in swarms, and she wanted the house quiet a while longer. She got up and poured the kettle water over a tea bag she didn't especially want, and carried the mug back to the table, and the warmth of it in her hands gave her the first idea she'd had all afternoon: heat was a thing. Not a condition, not a background feeling. A thing you could hold.

She pulled the scrap paper closer. The equation was exothermic, her notes said so, underlined twice in her own handwriting from Tuesday's class. And if the reaction was exothermic, then heat came out of it, the way heat came out of the mug into her palms. She wrote the equation again and then, after the products, in careful letters, added the word heat. Reactants on the left, products and heat on the right. It looked strange at first, like a sentence with a foreign word in it, and then it looked less strange, and then it looked obvious. If heat was a product, then raising the temperature was like adding more of a product, and she knew what the system did when you added a product. It pushed back. It shifted left, toward the reactants, consuming what she'd piled on.

She sat with that for a moment, testing it the way Ms. Fitzgerald had taught them to test everything, by turning it around. An endothermic reaction, then, would be the mirror image. She drew a bracket on her paper and wrote the word heat on the left side, among the reactants, and heat as a reactant meant that warming the system fed it, the same way adding any reactant did, and the equilibrium would shift right, toward the products, because that was where the added heat got used. Both cases in one picture. She had the sudden, unremarkable and enormous feeling of a door that had been locked all week swinging open on its own hinges.

The phone buzzed again and this time she picked it up. Carla had written a string of guesses about the homework, wrong ones, and Sophia called Alexe instead, because Alexe actually read the textbook instead of guessing. "Are you treating it as a thing?" Sophia asked, before hello. "Like it's in the equation." There was a pause, and the sound of Alexe moving to a quieter room, and then Alexe said, "Heat as a product of an exothermic reaction," and Sophia said, "Yes, exactly that," and for five minutes they talked over each other about the mirror case, endothermic, heat written in with the reactants, both of them laughing a little at how small the trick was and how long it had taken to find.

Her grandmother came down while Sophia was still on the phone, moving slowly along the counter with her hand flat on it, and put water in the kettle again without asking, because that was the economy of the house: whoever was up made the next pot. After Sophia hung up, her grandmother lowered herself into the other chair and looked at the scrap paper with its equations and the word heat written twice in Sophia's handwriting. "You've made it into an ingredient," her grandmother said, and Sophia started to correct her, to contextualize it, to say it was only a way of thinking, a bookkeeping device, and then she stopped, because she wasn't sure that was true. Maybe treating heat as a participant was just seeing what it had been all along.

She wasn't sure, either, whether the shift she'd predicted would be large or small, or how the exam would ask it, and she knew that knowing a way to think was not the same as having every answer. She wrote both equations out one more time in her notebook, clean, with arrows in both directions, and beside the second one she left a question mark, small and deliberate, a note to herself that something still waited to be understood. The kettle began its low murmur on the stove. "Two sugars," her grandmother said, already reaching for the pot.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
story:
Grayson set his laptop on the kitchen table between a bowl of cereal he was no longer eating and a chemistry textbook open to a chapter on enthalpy, the heat absorbed or released in a reaction, which he had a quiz on Monday. It was Saturday afternoon and the house was quiet. His mother had gone to his aunt's, and the dog was asleep under the table, quiescent in a way Grayson envied, because his group project was due at midnight and the code Mitchell had pushed to their shared repository would not compile.

He opened the file. Their assignment was to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then write tests for it, and Ms. Katz had split them into pairs on Thursday. Mitchell had written most of the Player class while Grayson was at track practice. The fields were fine, all private, but the getters were a mess. One field, score, had a getter called grabScore. Another, level, had retrieveLevel. A boolean field called active had a getter called checkIfActiveNow. Grayson read the method names twice, then tried to call grabScore in his test class and stared at the red underline that appeared.

He texted Mitchell first. "why not getScore?" Mitchell's reply came a few minutes later, from wherever he was on a Saturday. "works the same doesnt it." Grayson typed and deleted three responses. It did work the same, in the narrow sense that the program had run before, but reading the file was like reading a paragraph where every verb was conjugated differently. He could not say that without sounding like he was trying to vilify Mitchell for code that functioned, and Mitchell had done the fields correctly, which was more than Grayson had managed between Tuesday and Thursday.

Keisha was in the same class, and she had finished her project on Friday, alone, because she said partners cost her more time than they saved. He called her. "Every getter named differently," he said. "I can't tell what anything does without opening the whole file."

"What are the names?" She was chewing something. He read them off. There was a pause long enough that he checked whether the call had dropped.

"You don't invent getter names," she said. "There's a convention. A getter for a field named score is called getScore."

"And the boolean?"

"Usually with is. Like isActive."

He sat with that. It was not a rule the compiler enforced; he could see that already, because grabScore had run. It was something softer, an agreement about what words would mean, and the agreement only worked if everyone kept it. He opened Ms. Katz's slides from Monday, scrolled, and found a single line near the bottom that he had skimmed past: JavaBeans naming conventions. The same names Keisha had said, sitting there the whole time.

"I skimmed that slide," he said.

"Everybody did." Keisha told him about her own project, then asked about his weekend, then hung up because her brother needed the car. Grayson pushed back from the table and walked to the window over the sink, and while he stood there he was back in eighth grade for a moment, in his grandfather's garage, holding a wrench he did not know the size of. His grandfather had a wall of sockets arranged by width, and when Grayson asked why he didn't just throw them all in one drawer, his grandfather had said that you find things faster when they live where you expect. Grayson had thought this was about sockets. It had taken him until now to notice it was also about everything else.

He sat back down and made a list in his notebook: grabScore becomes getScore. retrieveLevel becomes getLevel. checkIfActiveNow becomes isActive. Then, before he changed anything, he texted Mitchell again, because the code was half Mitchell's and rewriting a partner's work without saying so seemed like its own kind of violation, the kind nobody writes a rule against but everybody feels. "I'm renaming the getters to the standard names. getScore, getLevel, isActive. It's a convention, not your code being wrong. Want me to push it so you can look?"

Mitchell's reply was a thumbs up and then, a minute later, "yeah sorry was rushing friday night." That was the whole apology, and Grayson found it was enough. He went through the file method by method, keeping the bodies untouched, changing only the names, and each time he renamed one he updated his test class to call the new name. The red underlines disappeared one by one. When he wrote the test for the boolean, he typed assertEquals(true, player.isActive()), and it read like a sentence, which it had not before.

He ran the tests. Two passed. One failed, and when he looked at it he found the failure was his own: in his test setup he had never called the method that set active to true, so the player was coming out inactive, and the test was reporting that honestly. He fixed the setup and ran them again, and the console printed three green marks, and the dog under the table lifted its head as though the small sound meant something.

He pushed the code and then, instead of closing the laptop, opened the chemistry chapter. Enthalpy had the same shape as the afternoon's problem, he thought, or maybe it didn't; it was heat either released or taken in, and you could not tell which just by looking, you had to know the convention for the sign. He read the first page and stopped comparing things.

At ten to midnight Mitchell pushed one more commit. Grayson pulled it and found the Player class had a new field, a boolean called ready, and below it, written in Mitchell's cramped style with no comment, a method called isReady.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
story:
Zoe had been putting it off for two days, which was long enough that Nika had started asking why she was being weird. They were at volleyball practice, doing passing drills in the far corner of the gym while Ms. Mehta worked with the front-row hitters at the net. Zoe kept the ball low between them, thirty passes, then switching, and on pass twenty-two she opened her mouth and then closed it.

The problem was Saturday's tournament. Nika had called for the ball on a broken play and then, when the set came, stood flat-footed and watched it drop. On the bus home Zoe had said, "You're lazy sometimes, you know that?" Nika had laughed, but not really. Since then Nika passed the ball back harder than the drill required, and answered questions with one word, and Zoe could feel the two of them drying out, some part of the friendship desiccating, and she did not know how to restart it.

She had gone looking, because that was what she did instead of sleeping. There was a handout from a leadership workshop her sister had left in the kitchen drawer, folded around a grocery receipt. It described something called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, and it framed feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. It gave an example: instead of "you're lazy," you said what happened on one occasion, what the person actually did, and what followed. Zoe had read it twice, then copied the three parts on her wrist in pen before practice.

It seemed almost too simple. But her mother talked about motivation the way a biologist might talk about a genotype, as if a person's character were fixed at the start and everything after was just the pattern expressing itself, and Zoe had absorbed that without ever deciding to. Lazy was a word like that. It named something inside Nika, permanent, invisible. The handout's way was different: it stayed outside, in the world, in things a camera could have seen. She did not know yet whether the second way was truer or just easier to say. Possibly both.

"Can I tell you something?" she said, catching a pass and holding it instead of returning it.

Nika stood with her hands on her hips. "You've been weird since Saturday."

"I know. Okay. Saturday, third set, when Lilianne called the broken play." Nika's chin came up, already braced for it. "You called for the ball, and then you didn't move your feet, so the set dropped between you and the ten-foot line, and we lost the point, and Lilianne had to cover for you on the next serve and got called for the lift."

Ms. Mehta blew her whistle across the gym. "Rotate!"

They walked to the next station, close enough to keep talking. "That's it?" Nika said. "No part where I'm a terrible person?"

"That's the whole thing. That's all I've got."

Nika took a ball off the cart and spun it once in her hands. "You could've said that on the bus."

"I know. Instead I said a word about your whole entire self, which, I looked this up, is like, it's not even about anything you did." Zoe rubbed her wrist, where the ink had smudged into three unreadable words. "It's called Situation-Behavior-Impact. You name the situation, the behavior, the impact. My sister's workshop thing."

"You wrote it on your arm."

"I wrote it on my arm."

Nika laughed for real this time, and then got quiet in a different way, the way she did when she was actually thinking. "My feet," she said. "Fine. That's fair, I do that." They set up for the hitting line, Nika behind Zoe now, and Zoe understood that the model was not magic, that saying it right did not guarantee anything, that Nika might still go flat in the next match. The handout had not promised that. It had only promised that you could aim at a moment instead of a person.

What Zoe could not decide was whether the reward mattered. If she was being kind to Nika in order to keep Nika, that was an extrinsic reason, a thing outside the thing itself, and it made the honesty feel slightly less honest. But standing in the hitting line, watching Nika call for the ball and actually move her feet, all the way through to the tape, Zoe thought maybe the distinction did not hold up. The kindness and the wanting were happening in the same body. She'd work that part out later, or she wouldn't.

"Set me," Nika said, slapping the ball into Zoe's hands. "And tell me if I drop my shoulder again. Like that. Say it exactly like that."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
Anais had signed up for the soup kitchen because her college applications wanted evidence of character, which she suspected was not what character was for, but the form did not offer a box for that. On her first Saturday she was assigned to the loading dock with Cierra, who had volunteered before and wore the certainty of someone who had. Behind them the industrial refrigerator hummed like a large animal pretending to be asleep. Cierra handed her a clipboard and said the first rule was never to denigrate the donors, even the ones who gave dented cans, because a dented can was still somebody's dinner.

The morning deliveries came in a slow procession: crates of bread, a pallet of pasta, bags of onions with the smell of earth still on them. Then the dairy van arrived, and the driver stacked four crates of milk directly on the dock before going to find the paperwork. The dock was warm. Anais put her hand against one of the cartons and it was not cold, and she thought about that, and then she thought about how long the driver had been gone.

"Those can't sit there," she said.

Cierra looked up. "He's coming back. It takes like two minutes."

But the driver was at the far end of the building arguing with someone about a gate code, and the minutes Cierra had promised kept not arriving. Anais stood between the crates and the door like a person guarding something, which, she realized, was exactly what she was. She knew the number from a food-safety pamphlet she had read the night before, mostly out of nerves, the way she read syllabi before the first day of school.

"Refrigerated food has to be kept at or below four degrees Celsius," she said. "Forty Fahrenheit. That's what keeps bacteria from growing fast." Cierra repeated it back to her, slowly, the way one memorizes a phone number, and then they were both crouched over the crates, lifting them two at a time, the cartons sweating in their hands.

In the kitchen, Ms. Weiss watched the milk go past on a cart. She had worked at the food bank for eleven years and had seen every variety of volunteer: the ones who photographed themselves ladling soup, the ones who cried, the ones who treated poverty as a personality they could try on for an afternoon. This one, the new girl, interested her, because the girl had stopped mid-dock and put her palm flat against a milk carton like a doctor taking a pulse. Ms. Weiss had once found a whole pallet of yogurt gone warm on that same dock, three summers ago, and had thrown it all out while a volunteer protested that it still smelled fine. She had never forgotten the smell of the dock at noon, the way the heat came up off the concrete like a breath.

She followed the cart into the cold room and asked the two girls where the milk had been. Cierra pointed. Ms. Weiss checked a thermometer against a carton, frowned at it, and said they had probably caught it in time, probably, and that word carried more weight than either of the girls understood.

"You did the right thing," she said to Anais. "Most people don't know the rule. Some of them don't want to."

Anais wanted to say that she hadn't known it either, twelve hours ago, and that the only reason she knew it now was anxiety dressed up as diligence. She said thank you instead. It seemed like the smaller dishonesty.

Later, in the crepuscular hour when the last guests had eaten and the folding tables were being wiped down, Alexe arrived to do the evening shift and told Anais about the regulars, which tables the quiet ones liked, which man always took two coffees and was not to be accused of anything for it. Alexe spoke about the guests with an easy fluency that made Anais feel like a tourist who had learned three phrases of a language. She had come here wanting to help and had spent the day mostly learning rules: temperatures, pallets, the fact that you did not hug anyone unless they hugged you first.

She kept thinking about the milk, about how close it had come. The driver had apologized, sort of, in the way of someone apologizing to the building rather than to a person. Ms. Weiss had accepted it with a nod that suggested she was keeping a file. Anais understood that the rule she had quoted was a small piece of a large machinery of care, and that most of that machinery was invisible until something rotted. She also understood that she still didn't know whether she was here for the applications or for the crates of milk, and she suspected that the answer might be both, and that both might be all right, though she could not yet say for certain.

She carried the last stack of clean trays toward the kitchen. Cierra was already outside on the dock, in the fading light, moving a single forgotten carton of orange juice off the concrete and into the cold.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
story:
The movers came on a Tuesday, and by Thursday Aiden was enrolled at Millbrook Secondary, standing in an office that smelled of photocopier ink while a woman with a lanyard printed his schedule. His old school had been a ten-minute bike ride from his house, close enough that he had never thought of it as separate from home. This one sat behind a ring road on the edge of a town he could not yet navigate without his phone.

At lunch he found the cafeteria and then lost his nerve at the door. He had rehearsed a version of himself who slid into any empty seat and started talking, but that person had been built out of six years of knowing everyone's name, and here he had nothing to stand on. He took his sandwich outside and ate it on a low wall facing the car park, watching two boys kick a tennis ball against a bin.

One of them, a tall boy called Tyler, came over on the third day and asked if he played football. Aiden said he was middling, which was honest, and Tyler said middling was fine, the Year 12 team was mostly middling. That became the shape of Aiden's days: training on Tuesdays, the wall at lunch on the other days, homework at the kitchen table while his mother unpacked boxes marked KITCHEN in his father's handwriting, since his father had stayed behind to sell the house and would follow in the spring.

The problem was the nights. He would lie in the unfamiliar acoustics of the new room, where the radiator ticked differently and traffic came from the wrong direction, and something would rise in his chest that he refused to name because naming it felt like losing. Back home he had been the one who was steady. Fabrice had cried at his own grandfather's funeral and Aiden had sat beside him and not said anything stupid, and Fabrice had told him afterwards that his quietness had helped. He wanted to be that person here too, and the thing in his chest argued with it.

Mr. Korhonen, who taught him English and lived, Tyler said, in the terraced house nearest the school, kept a shelf of paperbacks students could borrow. On Friday Aiden took one down at random, a thin book about the psychology of leaving home, mostly out of boredom, and read the middle pages standing up while the corridor emptied. What he found there stopped him. Nearly everyone who goes away from home misses something about it. That part was almost a relief. Then a harder sentence: roughly 20 percent of university students rated their homesickness at or above the midpoint of a severity scale.

He carried the number around through double maths. Twenty percent, one in five, which in a class of twenty-eight was five or six people, some severity scale he had no picture of but whose midpoint he suspected he had crossed the night he found himself listening to a recording of his old street's bus route on his phone. Not the worst case, then. Not even rare. But rare enough, apparently, that he had never once heard anyone at his old school admit to it, himself included, which meant all of them had been keeping the same secret and none of them had known.

He tested it out on Tyler the following Tuesday, screwing the cap off his water bottle with unnecessary care. "Did you know that nearly everyone who moves away misses something about home? And about twenty percent of uni students rate their homesickness at or above the midpoint of some severity scale." Tyler squinted at him. "Where'd you read that?" Aiden nodded toward his bag, where the paperback was wedged under his boots. Tyler was quiet for a moment, then said, "My cousin cried every night for a month her first term. She's the happiest person I know now." He kicked the ball back to the drill and added, over his shoulder, "Everybody misses something. Nobody says so."

Aiden wrote to Fabrice that night, not a confession exactly, more a letter that admitted the tick of the radiator and the wrong-direction traffic and the fact that he had been treating the whole thing as a private defect rather than an ordinary condition with an ordinary rate. Fabrice replied with a photograph of the bench outside their old school and one line: this is a synecdoche for everything you left, and it's still here. Aiden laughed out loud, alone in the room, and the laugh loosened something.

He could not decide, later, whether the statistic had enfranchised him or merely given him permission he should have had already, and he understood those might not be the same thing, and that the difference was one of the questions he was going to spend the next few years learning to ask. On Saturday he rode the bus route without his phone, learning the streets on purpose, and found that the unfamiliar light on unfamiliar brickwork had its own evanescent kind of beauty, there and gone as the bus passed. When he got home his mother asked how it was, and he said, "Better," and meant it in the unresolved, partial way that was, for now, the truest answer he had.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
story:
Gabriel had the exchange rate app open on his phone before he'd even put his backpack down. Six weeks ago, when Mr. Tran first proposed the economics trip to Lisbon, one euro had cost him a painful amount of dollars. Today the number was noticeably smaller. He sat at the kitchen counter and scrolled backward through the app's history, checking it twice, as if the graph might be lying to him.

"Whatever it is, no," his mother said, pulling a casserole dish from the oven.

"It's the euro. It got cheaper. Like, a lot." He turned the phone toward her. "Since April."

She glanced at it, unimpressed. "Good for you. Terrible for Portugal."

He was still chewing on that when Aisha texted him from the group chat, where the trip had become a full-time occupation: fundraising status, roommate lists, a spreadsheet Ashlyn had built that color-coded everyone's payment deadlines. Ashlyn had already requisitioned the spare funds from last year's car wash, and now she was hounding anyone whose row had gone red. Gabriel's row was red.

At school the next morning, Mr. Tran was taping a flyer to the classroom door. "Currency markets are having a moment," he said, in the tone of a man who considered this genuinely exciting. "You might watch the news tonight."

That was all the prompting Gabriel needed, which surprised him, because he had never thought of himself as the kind of person who watched the news for pleasure. But he did watch it that night, and then he read three articles, and then he read two of them again, because the first time through, the whole thing had sounded like a machine described by people who had never seen it. The central bank had raised interest rates. That was the part everyone agreed on.

He called Aisha. She answered with her mouth clearly full of something.

"Okay, so," he said. "Rates went up. And now money from other countries is flowing in, because you can earn more holding it here. All that foreign money coming in means our currency gets stronger."

A pause, some swallowing. "So the trip gets cheaper?"

"That's the part I'm figuring out. A stronger dollar means the euro's cheaper for us. And imports get cheaper too, which pushes prices down generally, which is the whole point, because inflation's been eating everyone alive." He stopped, aware that he had just talked for a very long time. "I think I finally get it."

"Congratulations on your one brain cell," Aisha said. "Tell Ashlyn, she's the one with the spreadsheet."

He told Ashlyn at lunch, and Ashlyn, who was quietly the most cerebral person he knew and hated being told so, looked up from her Tupperware with narrowed eyes. "So the bank raises rates, foreign money comes in, the currency strengthens, imports get cheaper, prices fall." She said it flatly, like she was checking his homework. "Fine. But here's my question. Does that help us or hurt us? We're not importing anything. We're importing Portugal."

"It helps us. The euro's cheaper for us. I checked the rate today."

"Then why is my row still red?" she asked, and returned to her salad with the finality of a judge.

By Thursday Gabriel had assembled what he considered a genuinely considered position: the rate cut was good for them as travelers, bad for his cousin who worked at an export company, and probably temporary, though the last part he couldn't back up with anything except a feeling. When his mother called him a revisionist for arguing, over dinner, that the trip should be booked immediately, before the effect wore off, he decided to take it as a compliment.

Friday afternoon, Mr. Tran stood at the front of the room with an expression Gabriel had learned to distrust. "Small update on Lisbon," Mr. Tran said. "The airline added a fuel surcharge."

Ashlyn's spreadsheet was out of her bag before he'd finished the sentence. "How much?"

"Enough that I'd ask everyone to check the new total."

Gabriel did the math in his head, the new rate against the new fee, the stronger dollar against the surcharge, and felt his entire considered position wobbling like a table on a bad floor.

Aisha leaned over from the next desk and looked at his calculator screen. "So," she said. "Still smarter than your one brain cell?"

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
story:
Xavier's father had taped a note to the fridge on Monday: scholarship applications close Friday, computer science section unfinished, the one that asked him to describe a technical concept in plain language. He had written and deleted four drafts. On Thursday evening he was still staring at a blank document when his phone buzzed with a message from Leonie: coming over, bringing the word list, you're going down.

She arrived at seven with her laptop bag over one shoulder and a paperback dictionary under her arm, the way other people brought snacks. "Ken's already setting up in your kitchen," she said, though she had texted him, not Xavier. "He wants to watch."

Ken was at the table with a bowl of cereal, and the dictionary lay open between them like a referee. The game was old, one they had played since middle school: a word was chosen, and each of them had to find it, Leonie in the million-entry word list on Xavier's laptop, Xavier in the printed dictionary. Except tonight Leonie had changed it. "New rule," she said. "We both use the laptop. Same list. You go your way, I go mine."

"Which is?"

"You'll see. Give me a word, Ken."

Ken scrolled with his thumb and said, "Perspicacious."

Xavier started at the top of the list, tabbing down through the A's, the B's, past para-, past per-, his eyes flicking line by line. Beside him Leonie did something strange: she jumped straight to the middle of the list, looked at the entry there, then jumped again, and again, and her hand came off the trackpad. "Found it," she said. "Perspicacious."

He had reached the P's. He kept going anyway, out of stubbornness, and found it forty seconds later in a silence that felt longer. "You got lucky," he said.

"I did not get lucky." She turned the laptop toward him. "Watch." She picked another word, then another, and each time she did the same halving thing, and each time she finished while he was still in the early letters. It felt like a trick, some artifice he couldn't see the wires of, and it bothered him more than losing, because he was the one applying to study this subject and he couldn't say what she was doing.

"How many times did you look at the screen?" he asked finally. "Actually count them."

She shrugged. "I wasn't counting. Count for me."

So he made her do it slowly, word by word, and he counted aloud. One entry in the middle. Then one in the middle of whichever half could contain the word. Then again. For a list of a million sorted entries, she never seemed to need more than twenty looks, and when he demanded to know why, she said, "Because halving a million twenty times leaves you one item. That's the whole thing. Ms. Kang showed us Tuesday. It's called a binary search." He had been sick Tuesday. He had missed one class and apparently the entire architecture of the possible.

"Whereas I was doing a linear search," he said. "One at a time, from the start."

"Which is fine if you enjoy suffering."

Ken, who had been quiet in the way of someone waiting to be asked, said, "Can I try the halving one?" and Leonie slid the laptop over without a glance. That was when Xavier understood something about the evening he hadn't planned to understand: Leonie hadn't come for the game. She had come because she wanted an audience, because Ms. Kang had told her she explained things well and she had been looking for someone to explain them to, and Xavier, tabbing through the A's like a man mowing a lawn with scissors, had been perfect.

He let that thought sit while he tested her. "Unsorted list," he said. "Random order. Does your halving still work?"

She paused, and he watched her want to say yes. "No," she admitted. "It has to be sorted. That's the catch. If the list isn't in order, you're stuck going one by one."

He nodded and opened his scholarship document. He typed a paragraph about two friends racing through a million-entry list, one checking in order and one halving, and about the twenty looks, and about the sort of problem where order itself is the price of speed. He read it over once. It was honest, which meant it included the part he hadn't resolved, whether it was better to be the person who knows or the person who can show someone else. Leonie was reading over his shoulder, which he decided not to mind.

"You put me in it," she said.

"Both of us."

Ken raised his hand like they were still in class. "One more word," he said, and scrolled with his thumb, grinning. "Obsequious. Go."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
story:
The tutoring centre occupied the back corner of the school library, four desks pushed together under fluorescent light that hummed like a trapped insect, and Maika had claimed the same seat every Tuesday since September because it faced the window and the ginkgo tree, which had gone from green to gold to bare in the time it took her to fail two calculus quizzes. She wanted, with a want that felt almost physical, to understand integration before the unit test on Friday. Not to memorize it. To understand it, the way she understood the smell of her grandmother's kitchen without being able to name a single ingredient.

Ms. Crowchild, who ran the centre, had a habit of eulogize the dead mathematicians as she walked between desks, praising Leibniz's handwriting one week and mourning Newton's grudges the next, and Maika had begun to think of her as a kind of undertaker for people whose ideas had outlived their feuds. Today Ms. Crowchild set a worksheet on the desk and moved on without comment, which Maika preferred. Comments felt like pressure. Worksheets were just paper.

Finnegan arrived late, as always, with his calculator in his back pocket and his application to engineering school half-finished in his head. He wanted the marks, not the mathematics, and he said so often, as though declaring it made the wanting less embarrassing. He dropped into the seat across from Maika and looked at her page upside down.

"That one's easy," he said. "You just add one to the exponent and divide by the new exponent. Power rule."

"I did that," Maika said. "For the first six. They're fine. It's this one." She turned the sheet so he could read it. The seventh problem was the integral of one over x, dx, and beside it she had written and crossed out x to the zero over zero, which looked, she thought, less like mathematics than like a small gravestone of its own.

Finnegan squinted. "So x to the negative one, add one, you get x to the zero, which is one, and you divide by zero." He sat back. "That's broken."

"That's what I got too."

"Then it's a typo. Skip it."

But Maika did not want to skip it, and this was the thing about her that Finnegan found quietly unnerving: she treated every broken problem as a door rather than a wall. Why would a textbook, this parsimonious institution that wasted no ink on anything untestable, devote a whole problem to something that divided by zero? Unless the division by zero was the point. Unless the rule was telling her, in the only way a rule could, where it stopped working. She sat with that thought while the fluorescent light buzzed and somewhere behind her Neha sharpened a pencil with slow, deliberate rotations, as if the pencil mattered.

Neha slid her chair over. She had come to the centre for physics help and stayed for the company, a kind of symbiosis Maika had noticed in the room generally: the strong students grew stronger by explaining, the weak ones survived by being explained to, and everyone pretended the arrangement was friendship, which after a while it actually was. Neha leaned over Maika's shoulder, and the smell of her mint gum arrived before her voice did.

"Try ln," Neha said.

"Try what?"

"Ln. My cousin in first year said it. For this exact one. She said the antiderivative of one over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x." Neha shrugged, as if to disown the sentence now that it was out of her.

Finnegan frowned. "That's not a rule. That's a rumour."

"It fills the gap," Neha said. "The power rule can't do it. This can."

Maika wrote it out. The integral of one over x, dx, equals the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, plus C, because there was always a plus C, that small admission that antiderivatives were families and not individuals. She tested it against the picture in her head, the curve of one over x falling away from its asymptote, and the area accumulating beneath it, and she tried to imagine what shape of number would grow slowly enough to measure that region without ever quite catching up. A logarithm grew slowly. She knew that from graphing unit, though she had never before had a reason to care.

"Ms. Crowchild," she called, before she could decide not to. "Is this right?" She held up the sheet, the way a person holds up a fish they are not sure is legal.

Ms. Crowchild came over, read the line, and did something Maika had never seen a teacher do in the moment of confirming an answer: nothing at all. No nod, no smile, no checkmark. She simply tapped the edge of the page twice and walked away toward the window and the bare ginkgo, and Maika understood the two taps the way she understood her grandmother's kitchen.

Finnegan was quiet for a long minute, working something through with his pen cap between his teeth. Then he said, "Okay. I take back the typo thing." He pulled the worksheet toward himself and copied the line into his own notes, carefully, adding a bracket around the absolute value because he was the sort of person who believed a well-placed bracket would save him on Friday. "I still think it's weird that a whole new function shows up just because one exponent went wrong. Like the power rule has this one soft spot and log lives there."

"That's not weird," Maika said. "That's my favourite part." She looked at the line again, at the small gap it filled, and she thought about how much of what she'd been taught had arrived seamless and confident, and how the seamlessness had been a kind of lie, because every rule had a place where it ended and something else began. She did not know yet what to do with that knowledge. She suspected it would matter more outside this room than inside it.

Neha blew a bubble and popped it. "So what happens at x equals zero?"

Maika looked at the asymptote on her sketch, the place where the curve fled upward off the page and the logarithm was not invited. "I don't know," she said, and started a new problem.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
The phone repair shop smelled of solder and lemon cleaner, and behind the counter Bentley was arguing with a recalcitrant tablet that refused to charge no matter how he angled the cable. Alexa sat on the stool by the register with her laptop open, a tutorial half loaded, because Mr. Bélanger had offered her the evening shift's slow hours to practice. He wanted a simple answer by closing time: which customers in his little database had brought in a device for repair but never bought a single accessory, no case, no screen protector, nothing. He called them his ghosts, and he said it cheerfully, the way other people talked about weather.

The tables sat there on her screen like two orderly streets. One held customers, each with an ID and a name. The other held orders, each tied to a customer by that same ID. She had learned the shape of a LEFT JOIN that morning: every customer, and beside each one, whatever orders matched, or nothing where nothing matched. The nothing was the point. The ghosts lived in the gaps.

She typed the join first, feeling the logic settle like a solved lock. Then the condition. She paused, wondering whether a person could write a question so politely that the database would simply tell the truth, and wrote WHERE order_id = NULL, because the ghost rows would have nothing in the order column, and nothing, surely, was the same as NULL. She ran it. Zero rows. She ran it again, as though the machine might reconsider. Zero rows, and the little timer at the bottom of the window said the query had taken two milliseconds, so it had looked, and found, and returned nothing with total confidence.

"You look like the tablet feels," Bentley said from behind the counter, holding the charging cable up like evidence.

"It's not working and it's not wrong," Alexa said. "That's a bad combination." She scrolled the results pane anyway, in case rows were hiding. They weren't. Somewhere in her tutorial folder there was a screenshot of a similar query, she remembered, with a difference she hadn't understood at the time. She found it. The WHERE clause there didn't say equals NULL. It said something else, shorter and stranger: IS NULL. She said it out loud, quietly, tasting the grammar of it. Not a comparison at all. A statement of being.

"It's like asking if a fjord is equal to a valley," she said, mostly to herself, watching Bentley plug the tablet in at a third angle. "The question doesn't even get asked. That's different from the answer being no." She wasn't sure the image held, but she liked it enough to keep it. She changed one line, swapping = NULL for IS NULL, and pressed enter.

Eleven rows came back. Eleven ghosts, each with a name and a blank where the order should be, printed down the screen like light through a shutter. She read the names and recognized two of them, regulars who came in for screen repairs and always waved off the accessory case by the register with the same small shake of the head. So the machine had found something true that Mr. Bélanger already half knew, and had also found nine he didn't. She copied the list into an email, then stopped before sending it.

Elie pushed through the door with rain on her jacket and a cracked phone in her hand, and leaned over Alexa's shoulder. "You could have just asked him who never buys anything."

"But then it's his memory," Alexa said. "This way it's his records. Those are different things and I don't know which one he trusts more." She was aware of holding both ideas at once, the way she'd once held two contradicting readings of the same poem in English class, refusing to pick. The database said these eleven people ordered nothing. But NULL, she had just learned, didn't mean never; it meant unknown, an absence of record rather than a record of absence. Some of the eleven might have bought a case in cash, off the books, back when Mr. Bélanger's daughter was minding the register. The query answered exactly what it was asked and nothing more, and Alexa respected that narrowness suddenly, the way she respected a friend who never gossiped.

Mr. Bélanger came out from the back wiping his hands on a rag and read the list over her other shoulder, lips moving slightly. He didn't denigrate the ghosts, though she half expected him to, calling them cheapskates or browsers. Instead he tapped one name, a woman who had come in every winter for three years with a dying battery, and said, "She buys her cases online, I think. Cheaper. Can't blame her." Then he tapped another and frowned, genuinely puzzled, which Alexa thought was the best thing the query had produced: not an answer but a small honest not-knowing, eleven of them in a column.

"Send it," he said. "I'll ask a couple of them what they use instead." Elie's phone was already on the counter, its fracture map catching the shop's fluorescent light, and Bentley finally held up the tablet, screen glowing, triumphant. Alexa hit send on the email, then saved the query with a filename she liked: ghosts, lowercase. Below it she typed a second line for tomorrow, a wondering she hadn't solved yet, a way to tell a true nothing from an unknown one, and left the cursor blinking after it.

story:
Violet got to the counter at 4:40, ordered a small drip coffee she did not particularly want, and took the table by the window because the outlet there worked. Samira arrived eight minutes later with Ms. Van Dijk's worksheet folded into quarters, which she unfolded across the sugar stains and smoothed flat with the heel of her hand. Four boxes were drawn along the top: A, K, 4, 7. Above them the rule was printed in bold: If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side.

"Leo picked A and 4," Samira said. "So did I, when she first showed it to us. So did almost everybody."

Violet read the instructions again. Turn over only the cards you need to test whether the rule is true. She had missed the class on Tuesday because of the orthodontist, and the quiz on Thursday covered it, and Ms. Van Dijk had said, without any warmth, that the class average suggested they had not understood the assignment. Samira had texted her a photo of the board afterward: Wason, 1966. The number had stuck because Samira had underlined it twice.

"A and 4," Violet said. "You look at the A, because if there's an odd number behind it the rule's dead. Then the 4, because if there's a consonant behind it, it's also dead."

"That's what we all said. But Ms. Van Dijk said a consonant behind the 4 doesn't matter. The rule only says what happens after a vowel. A consonant can have anything behind it. Odd, even, whatever. The rule doesn't promise anything about consonants."

Violet turned her cup a quarter rotation. Behind the window the light had gone crepuscular, the parking lot lamps not yet on, everything a flat grey. She drew the four cards on a napkin and wrote underneath each one everything it could possibly show. Behind the A: an even number, fine, or an odd number, rule broken. Behind the K: anything at all, fine no matter what. Behind the 4: a vowel, fine, or a consonant, fine, because the rule made no claim about even numbers and what was on their other side. Behind the 7: a vowel, which would break the rule, or a consonant, fine.

"So the 7," she said. "You turn the A and the 7."

"Which is what fewer than ten percent of the people in the study did," Samira said. "In the abstract version. That's what she kept saying. He called it the selection task, Peter Wason, and he ran it in 1966, and almost everyone got it wrong." She tapped the worksheet. "She said our class did slightly worse than that, actually, which she seemed to enjoy."

The door chimed and Leo came in with his backpack still on one shoulder. He bought a hot chocolate and pulled a chair over without asking. "Are we still doing this? I have to relearn this by Thursday or I'm finished."

"It's not memorizing," Violet said. "I did it on a napkin. You have to ask what each card could hide, not what you expect to find." She slid the napkin across. "Everyone wants to turn the 4 because they turn it into a different rule in their head. Like, if there's an even number, there's a vowel. But that's not the rule on the page."

Leo leaned over the napkin. "So the 7 could have a vowel behind it."

"And then the rule's false. But if it has a consonant, you learned nothing, which is fine, because you weren't promised anything."

He sat back. "It's like the thing my dad does with the insurance forms. He's always saying the contract won't indemnify them for the flood damage, it only covers fire, and everyone signs it assuming it covers both. The words only go one direction."

Violet looked at him. She had known Leo since seventh grade and had never heard him reference his father's work once. "That's the same shape," she said slowly. "The rule only goes one direction too. If vowel, then even. Not if even, then vowel."

Samira said, "She'll ask us tomorrow why the drinking-age version is easier. If a person is drinking beer, they have to be over twenty-one, and everyone picks the right cards when it's about people instead of letters. Almost nobody picks right with the letters."

"But she won't tell us why the letters are harder?"

"She said we can propose theories, but she wouldn't confirm any of them. She said, 'The data are the data.'"

"That's a contrivance," Leo said. "Making us figure it out so it sticks better."

"Maybe," Violet said. She took the napkin back and drew a second set of four boxes, then a third. She could see the logic now, could walk it card by card, and she could also see that walking it was not the same as knowing why her mind had wanted the 4 in the first place. That part she could not yet account for. She wrote A and 7 under the last set of boxes, then folded the napkin and put it in her pocket.

Samira checked the time. "I have to be home by six."

"We're here tomorrow at four," Violet said. "Same table. Bring the drinking version."

story:
Benjamin arrived at his aunt's house with the Haggadah in his backpack and the printout of the order of service folded into quarters, which he had annotated in three colors of ink. His grandfather had led the Seder every year of Benjamin's life, his voice low and exact, pausing at each turn of the page like a man crossing a stream on stones he had memorized. This year his grandfather was in the hospital with something the adults called minor in the tone they reserved for things that were not, and Benjamin's mother had said, at dinner two weeks before, "You know it better than the rest of us. You should do it." He had said yes before he had thought about what yes would require.

The house was loud before it was anything else. Cousins ran through the hallway trailing a toy ambulance, his uncle argued pleasantly with the cashier from his deli about a shipment of brisket, and Guneet, who had come because her own family was traveling, stood in the kitchen holding a jar of horseradish and asking whether it was a sauce or a punishment. Benjamin had invited Mahmoud too, back in February, imagining a quiet evening. He had since been disabused of that fantasy by every Passover he had ever attended, and yet here they both were, at the arboreal edge of the yard, where his aunt's enormous fig tree dropped last year's leaves onto the patio furniture nobody had yet uncovered.

The first stumble came early. He had the stack of matzah in front of him, and he reached for it, and then stopped, because he could not remember whether the blessing came before or after the breaking. At home he had drilled the sequence, but the sequence lived in his notebook, and his notebook was in the backpack, and the backpack was by the door, and the door was very far away suddenly. His grandmother watched him with an expression he could not read. He looked at his mother, who shrugged in a way that meant either it doesn't matter or figure it out, and those were, he understood, two entirely different shrugs.

He got through it by guessing, and then during the meal he excused himself, went to the hallway, and texted his grandfather. Which step after the sandwich, he typed, then deleted it, then typed, Are you allowed to have your phone in there. The reply came in four minutes, all capitals: SANDWICH THEN THE AFTERMATZAH THEN WE OPEN THE DOOR FOR ELIJAH. Then a second message: YOU KNOW WHY IT'S CALLED SEDER. Benjamin stared at it. He did know, and he had known for years without ever letting it matter: the festive meal was called a Seder, a Hebrew word meaning order, because its rituals followed a fixed sequence from start to finish. That was the whole idea. Not the food, not the singing even, but the order itself, the same order his grandfather had kept every spring like a man keeping a promise whose original terms he had inherited rather than chosen.

Back at the table, Guneet asked him why he kept checking a folded piece of paper like a student smuggling notes into an exam. Mahmoud laughed, and Benjamin found he could not decide whether he was embarrassed or grateful, and settled on both. "It's called a Seder," he said. "It means order. That's the whole point of tonight." Guneet nodded slowly, the way people nodded at things they intended to think about later.

The quagmire arrived with the Four Questions, which by tradition the youngest asks. The youngest at the table was six and knew only the first two, so Benjamin started to recite the rest himself, and his grandmother stopped him with a raised hand and said, in Hebrew, that the questions were not his to ask. His mother said they could be shared. His uncle said something about how in his house growing up, nobody had asked anything, which got a bigger laugh than it probably deserved. Benjamin sat in the middle of it and understood, with a clarity that surprised him, that his grandfather's way, everything in its turn, and his mother's way, everyone in the conversation, were not opposites but two hands on the same cup, and that he did not yet know which hand he was.

He made a decision he could not fully defend. He let the six-year-old sing what she knew. He sang the rest. Then he opened the front door for Elijah, and the night air came in carrying the smell of the fig tree and the neighbor's dryer, and for a moment nobody at the table spoke, all of them watching the empty doorway as if the order of things might walk through it.

When they got to the last cup, his grandmother touched his wrist and said, "Your grandfather will be jealous." Benjamin looked down at his place setting, at the wine he was technically allowed four sips of and had been rationing all night, and said, "Tell him it was messier than his."

"Good," she said, and reached for the matzah.

activity: going on a first date
story:
The rink smelled like cold rubber and syrup from the snack bar, and Mason had been standing at the skate counter for four minutes trying to look like a person who knew what he was doing. His date, a girl from his chemistry class whose name tag at the rental desk said nothing because she didn't work there, was already lacing up. He had planned this for two weeks. He had even practiced stopping, once, in his driveway, in his socks, which had not augured well.

"You're wobbling," she said, delighted. Her name was Prue, and she skated like the floor owed her money.

"I'm loosening up," said Mason, which was a lie so transparent that even his skates seemed embarrassed.

By the second lap he had found a rhythm, and by the fourth he had found her hand, and things were going so well that he almost didn't notice the first time she grabbed his arm. She was laughing at something, a kid in a dinosaur helmet who had fallen in a perfect slow spiral, and she clamped his forearm to steady herself. It hurt in a small, specific way, like a blood pressure cuff with a sense of humor. He filed it under enthusiasm.

In the stands, Pedro and Felix-Antoine were sharing a plate of nachos they had no business calling nachos, since the cheese had gone the consistency of caulk. They had come, officially, to "support the arts," and unofficially because neither had anything else to do on a Thursday.

"Watch," said Felix-Antoine, gesturing with a chip. "She keeps doing that. The arm thing."

"Doing what?"

"Grabbing him. Hard. That's the third time. Look at his face after."

Pedro watched. Mason's face did a little thing after each grab, a wince smoothed over fast, the way you'd react to a stone in your shoe mid-introduction. "Huh," said Pedro. He had spent the whole semester in a health elective nobody else wanted, and something surfaced in him now, the way a license plate number surfaces when the police ask. "We just did this unit. In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence." He said it flat, like he was reading it off the nachos.

"That's grim," said Felix-Antoine.

"That's one kid in every row of the bleachers, basically." Pedro set down the chip. "I'm not saying that's this. She might just be clingy on skates."

"Everything is clingy on skates. It's the whole business model of skating."

Down on the floor, Prue grabbed Mason's arm again, hauling herself around the turn, and this time he said, "Ow, actually," and she laughed and let go, and thirty seconds later did it again. He began, quietly, to keep his left side angled away from her, a maneuver that required more skating acumen than he possessed, and which resulted in his colliding gently with a support column.

He skated over to the boards near his friends, pretending to fix his laces.

"You good?" said Pedro.

"Great," said Mason. Then, lower: "Does she grab hard, or am I being a baby?"

Felix-Antoine opened his mouth with the confidence of a man about to be scathing, and Pedro elbowed him before he could deploy it. "You're not being a baby," Pedro said. "She's leaving marks on your arm. I have eyes and, unlike Felix, I use them."

"Okay, one time I ignored a stop sign."

"It was a roundabout."

Mason looked at his forearm, where four pink ovals were surfacing, fading, surfacing again like a poorly edited photograph. He had spent two weeks rehearsing conversation topics, among them whether soup was a beverage, and had somehow rehearsed nothing for this. On one hand: it was a first date, she was funny, the kid in the dinosaur helmet had waved at him. On the other: one in twelve. It wasn't a law of the universe, it was just a number some survey had found, and it didn't say whether this was that, or whether Prue was that, and a number couldn't tell you what to say to a girl holding your arm.

He went back out anyway. He waited until she reached for him, and then, as gently as he could manage at nine miles an hour, he said, "Hey, you can hold my hand. Just, the arm thing hurts a little. My arms are famously made of dough."

Prue blinked. She looked, for a second, like someone checking a map. "Oh," she said. "Sorry. I do that when I'm nervous. I didn't think."

"Okay," said Mason. "Well. Now you think."

"Now I think," she agreed, and took his hand instead, much more carefully, like it was something she was being trusted with, and the kid in the dinosaur helmet went by again, waving, still falling, completely unbothered.

"IS SOUP A BEVERAGE?" Mason called over the music, because he had rehearsed it, and because a moment ago the night could have gone anywhere.

"Obviously not," said Prue. "Rerack. Wrong question."

"Fine. IS A SMOOTHIE A SOUP?"

She squeezed his hand once, hard, and then remembered, and loosened it.
