story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and cold concrete, and Caleb had claimed the corner by the workbench because it was the one place in the house where nobody asked what he was doing. He had his phone propped against a coffee tin, a keyboard app glowing on the screen, and staff paper weighted down with his father's abandoned socket wrench set. Sixteen bars. Chord changes. Written notation. The assignment sheet from Mr. Leblanc sat beside his elbow, dog-eared already.

The trouble was that Caleb could hear music all day, whole cascades of it, but the moment he tried to trap a phrase on paper, it went stiff, like a beetle pinned in a display case. He had worked out four bars the night before, a simple melody over a repeated pattern, and by bar eight the whole thing wanted to stop. It sounded finished. That was the problem. It sounded finished at exactly the wrong moment, and he had ten more bars to fill.

Alistair arrived on his bike with the noiseless confidence of someone who had been told the garage door was open and never questioned it. He leaned over the staff paper, chewing the strap of his helmet. "It just quits," he said. "Like a sentence with no period. No, wait. Like a sentence with all periods."

Caleb played the eight bars again, slower, listening past his own fingers. The last chord had a settled, square-jawed quality, the sound of a door closing on a room nobody had entered yet. He kept circling it the way he circled a math problem he suspected had a cleaner solution than the one he'd found. What if the ending was the thing doing the damage? What if the phrase wanted to be left hanging?

Agatha appeared in the doorway with two cans of soda and an opinion, as usual, about both. She had taken music theory the year before, the year Caleb had dismissed as paperwork for people who couldn't actually play. He had since revised this position, quietly, without announcing the reversal. She set a can on the workbench, condensation already sweating onto the staff paper, and he moved it with the speed of someone rescuing a small animal.

"Play the end," she said. He played it. "Now instead of that last chord, put the five chord there. The one built on the fifth note." He tapped it into the keyboard app, and the garage changed temperature, or seemed to. The phrase stopped asking to be finished and started asking to be continued. "It's called a half cadence," Agatha said, cracking her soda. "Ends on the five chord. Sounds unfinished on purpose."

"A trap," Alistair said, delighted. "You're setting a trap for the listener."

Caleb wrote the chord in, then played all eight bars twice more, and the second time he felt the pull in his own chest, the leaning-forward feeling of wanting the next phrase. He had always thought of theory as a set of rules for propitiating some grim examiner, an offering of correct spellings and roman numerals, but this was something else, closer to chicanery in the best sense, a trick played openly, the audience invited in on it and fooled anyway. He wondered whether a whole piece could be built out of doors that opened onto more doors.

Mr. Leblanc found them there an hour later, having walked over from his house two doors down, ostensibly about the hedge that bordered both properties. He stood in the garage doorway with his hands in his pockets, noxious fumes from a neighboring yard's leaf blower drifting past him, and listened while Caleb played the eight bars, then the nine, then the twelve he had started sketching in pencil so light it was almost rumor.

"You left the eighth bar hanging," Mr. Leblanc said. It wasn't a question.

Caleb looked at the paper. "I did it on purpose," he said, and heard how it came out, half defiant, half asking to be believed. He was not entirely sure which half was true. He had done it on purpose, and he also suspected he would not have thought of it if the melody had not stopped on its own first, and he could not separate those two things no matter how he turned them over. Some discoveries you made and some made you, and the middle of the Venn diagram was where he seemed to live.

"Then write the next phrase like you mean to pay it off," Mr. Leblanc said, and nodded at the hedge as though resuming a conversation that had never stopped. "It leans on the fence between our yards, you know. Yours can lean too."

Caleb picked up the pencil. Alistair leaned in over his shoulder, and Agatha pulled the second chair around, and the garage light hummed its one long note above them while Caleb wrote bar thirteen.

story:
The envelope from Aldersgate College had arrived on a Tuesday, and by Thursday Dominic had been summoned to the guidance office, which smelled like instant coffee and the fake pine of December. He sat across from Mr. Adebayo with the letter folded in his back pocket, its crease already soft from handling. On the desk between them lay a scatter of transcript printouts and a half-eaten clementine, its peel curled like a ribbon.

"Congratulations," Mr. Adebayo said, though Dominic had not yet said the word accepted out loud. "Early Action. You applied in the fall, they answered in December, and now you have an answer before most people have even finished their forms." He slid a form across the desk, the one for the regular decision applications to Hartwell and Cass Technical and the state school, the ones whose deadlines were still two weeks away.

"I was thinking I'd just not do these," Dominic said. He tried to verbalize the feeling behind it, the way the letter had made everything feel finished, decided, over. "Like, I got in. Why keep writing essays about a challenge I overcame?"

"It's not binding," said a voice from the doorway. Maira stood there holding a folder someone had sent her to deliver, and she did not leave, because Maira never left anywhere quickly. "Early Action. You get an early decision but you can still say no. My sister did it. She got admitted in December and enrolled somewhere else entirely in April, and nobody revoked anything."

Dominic looked at her, then at Mr. Adebayo, who had leaned back with the particular stillness of a man letting two sixteen-year-olds work something out. The letter in his pocket felt suddenly less like an ending and more like a floor, something to stand on rather than a ceiling he had hit.

"So I could go anywhere," he said slowly. "Or I could go there."

"You could," Maira said. She set the folder on the corner of the desk, straightening it against the edge, an old habit of hers from three years of shelving books at the library. "That's what my sister said was the worst part, actually. Having the choice."

Mr. Adebayo watched the two of them while pretending to review the transcript printouts. He had been doing this job long enough to know that second-semester juniors and first-semester seniors occupied different taxonomies entirely, and Dominic had migrated between them in the space of one letter. He had also learned that the urge to rescue a student from a decision was endemic to his profession, an impulse he had to fight the way a doctor resists prescribing antibiotics for a cold. The boy did not need rescuing. He needed a deadline and a sandwich, probably.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," Dominic said. He had pulled the letter out now, holding it flat on his knee like a card he might play. "If Aldersgate is good, and it is good, then finishing the other applications is just work for no reason. But if I don't finish them, then Aldersgate stops being a choice and becomes the only thing. And I liked it better when it was a choice." He paused. "I don't know if that makes sense."

"It makes sense," Maira said. "It's just not a reason. It's a feeling wearing a reason's clothes."

Mr. Adebayo laughed despite himself, and the clementine peel rolled off the desk, and Maira bent to pick it up before it hit the floor, dropping it into the trash can by the filing cabinet without comment. She took the empty plate with her when she left, carrying it like it was the folder she'd originally come for, and the door sighed shut behind her.

Dominic sat for another minute in the quiet she had left. Then he picked up the Hartwell form, clicked Mr. Adebayo's pen twice out of habit, and at the top of the line where it asked for his intended major, he wrote undecided.

"Both of them?" Mr. Adebayo asked, nodding at the Cass Technical form still waiting.

"Both of them," Dominic said, and started the second essay.

story:
The permission slip had said Family Meal Night, and Nolan had read it three times on the bus, because in his house nobody needed a permission slip to eat. His mother worked the evening shift at the hospital, his father sent a remittance from the job up north every second Friday, and his little brother, Dev, mostly lived on cereal. So the idea of cooking an actual dinner for them, in Mr. Bennett's room with its six stoves and hanging steel pans, had seemed at first like something borrowed from a different family. He had signed the slip anyway, and chosen roast chicken, because that was the dish his father used to make on Sundays before the job took him away.

He was not alone in the room. Haley had claimed the station beside his and was assembling a lasagna with the confidence of someone who had already litigated the question of ricotta versus béchamel with Carlo, who sat on the counter eating raw mushrooms and offering verdicts. The families would arrive at six. The clock above the door said five-forty, which Nolan tried not to look at, and then looked at anyway.

He unwrapped the chicken, set it in the sink, and turned on the tap. It was what his father did. He could still see it: the deliberate rinse, the water running pale over the pale skin, the shake, the paper towels, as though the bird arrived dirty, the way anything from a market arrived dirty. Dev, who had come early because the middle school let out first and he had nowhere else to go, grabbed his arm before the water touched it.

"Don't," Dev said. "The CDC says not to wash raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the counters. It's on the wall over there."

Nolan looked. Taped beside the handwashing poster was a printed page, the blue logo of the CDC at the top, and the same words Dev had said, plus a few he hadn't: nearby surfaces, not just the sink. He turned off the tap with two fingers. "Then how does it get clean?"

"It gets clean when you cook it," Dev said, in the tone of a person who had read the page twice and intended to enjoy this for the rest of the year.

Nolan stood there with a raw chicken and a problem. His father's method was not just a method; it was a kind of grammar, the way the man did everything, rinsed and dried and salted as if care itself were the point. But his father was four hundred miles away, and the evidence was on the wall, and Dev was watching him with his chin up, waiting to see which authority his older brother would obey.

He did both, in a way. He patted the chicken dry with paper towels, salted it the way his father did, sliding his thumb under the skin over the breast, and set it in the pan his father would have chosen. Then he took out his phone.

He typed: Doing the chicken for Family Meal Night. Did you know you're not supposed to wash it? CDC says the splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the nearby surfaces. I'm not washing it. Still doing the thing under the skin with the butter and the thyme.

The reply came while the chicken was going into the oven, and it was longer than his father's messages usually were. His father wrote like a man paying by the word. This one said: Your grandmother washed it and her mother before her. Never made anyone sick that I heard of. But they didn't have the science, and I don't either, so if the CDC says the water spreads it around the kitchen, do what they say. The rest, the butter, keep that. That part isn't science. It's just ours.

Nolan read it twice and put the phone face down on the steel counter, and Haley looked over and said, "Bad news?" and he said, "No," and found that he meant it.

The families arrived at six, and his mother came in her scrub top with her hair still damp, and his father came in behind her, which was the twist Nolan had not been told to expect, a Friday visit nobody had mentioned, and for a second Nolan stood very still at his station with the carving knife in his hand. Then Dev bolted across the room and their father caught him, and over Dev's shoulder he looked at the oven, at the browning skin, at the two of them.

"Did you wash it?" his father asked, coming over, not touching anything, the way he never touched anything in kitchens that weren't his.

"No," Nolan said. "The water splashes and spreads bacteria. To the sink, the counters, everything nearby. It's a CDC thing." He opened the oven and pulled the pan out, and the steam came up between them, smelling of thyme and butter and the exact Sundays Nolan had been afraid he was losing. "Everything else I did your way."

His father leaned in over the steam, closed his eyes for a moment, and said, "Then carve it, and don't give your brother the wing, he complains."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
The nurse's office had been converted into a screening station for the health fair, and Luke stood at the second table with a cuff in his hands, waiting for Ms. Gill to finish with the student before him. She was the biology teacher who had organized the whole thing, and she had drafted six seniors to run the tables after a single afternoon of training. The cuff was heavier than he expected. It smelled like the inside of a doctor's waiting room, that faint powder and plastic smell, and when he squeezed the bulb it gave back nothing, just air moving through a tube.

Luke's job was simple on paper. Wrap the cuff, rest the person's arm on the table, inflate until the gauge climbed past one-forty, then ease the pressure down and listen. Two numbers. He wrote them on a card and handed it over. The hard part, Ms. Gill had said, was what came after the numbers, because people would ask what they meant, and he was supposed to say, "That's a question for your doctor," unless they pressed, and then he could tell them what the numbers measured without pretending to know more than he did. She had made them practice that sentence until it sounded bored instead of defensive.

He got through the morning on routine. Walter took a turn in the chair and let the cuff hiss against his arm while Maddex read out the gauge for him, and they argued about whether the fifth sound or the disappearance of it was the lower number, and Luke told them to check the card Ms. Gill had laminated, which said the disappearance, and they checked, and it did. Around eleven the parents started arriving for the open house portion, and the tables got busier, and the questions got harder.

A man in a gray jacket sat down at Luke's table a little after noon and pushed up his sleeve without being asked. He said he was somebody's father, gesturing vaguely toward the gymnasium doors, and that he hadn't had a reading in years because he didn't like what doctors had to say. Luke wrapped the cuff the way he'd been taught, two fingers of slack, the arrow over the artery, and pumped. The needle swung up and came down, and he listened, and wrote the numbers on the card and turned it around.

The man looked at the card for a long moment and asked if it was bad.

Luke said it was high, and that a doctor was the one to say how high, and the man said that was exactly the kind of answer that let people like him go home and forget about it. He said it without heat, more tired than anything, and Luke found he couldn't retreat behind the laminated sentence. He said the two numbers were pressure in the arteries, the higher one when the heart beat, the lower one between beats, and that the man's were above where they should sit.

"So what do I do," the man said. "Am I supposed to take a pill and eat like a rabbit."

Luke had a page of notes from the training folded in his pocket, and he took it out, and the relevant line was one Ms. Gill had underlined twice, about exercise. He read it once to himself and then put the notes away, because reading to a man's face felt like hiding. "Regular aerobic exercise lowers blood pressure in a lot of people," he said. "Brisk walking, or cycling, on most days. Even people who already have hypertension." The word felt strange in his mouth, formal, but the man nodded like it was a word he'd heard before in other rooms.

"You mean like walking around the block."

"Like walking fast enough that you couldn't sing but you could still talk," Luke said, and the man almost smiled at that, said his wife had been saying the same thing in different words for a decade.

Walter drifted over during the lull and leaned on the table, and when the man went to find his son, Walter said Luke had just prescribed exercise to a stranger. Luke said he hadn't prescribed anything, he'd read a line off a card, and Walter said it hadn't sounded like a card, it had sounded like Luke meant it. That stopped Luke for a second. He had meant it. Somewhere between reading the line and saying it, the sentence had become his, and he was circumspect about that, because the training had been clear about where his knowledge ended and a clinic's began, and yet the ending felt thinner than the middle.

He tried to compartmentalize it on the walk to the cafeteria, filing the man's face under finished business, but it wouldn't file. What stayed was the man's question, "Am I supposed to take a pill and eat like a rabbit," and the way it assumed the only choices were drastic ones, and how the alternative Luke had offered was almost insultingly small, most days, a brisk walk, and yet small was the whole point. He didn't know whether the man would do it. He didn't know whether one reading on a folded table in a hallway meant anything at all, or whether it was an indictment of the whole setup, six seniors with an afternoon of training telling parents things that deserved a follow-up appointment nobody would schedule.

After school Ms. Gill found him stacking chairs and asked how the day had gone. He told her about the man, the numbers, the line about walking. She listened with her arms crossed, and when he finished she didn't correct him or praise him, she just asked whether he'd told the man to see a doctor. He said he had, twice, and the man had said sure, and Luke hadn't believed him. Ms. Gill considered that, and said the reading they didn't measure was whether anything changed afterward, and no table at any health fair could take it.

On his way out through the side doors, Luke saw the man again, across the parking lot, standing beside a sedan with a boy who had to be his son, the two of them not talking, just waiting for the lot to clear. The man had the card in his hand, turning it over. Luke stood by the doors with his bag on his shoulder, and after a moment the man folded the card once and put it in the pocket of the gray jacket, and unlocked the car.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
story:
Jessica had spread her books across the long table by the library window before Isaiah arrived, two of them open to the same decade and disagreeing about it. One historian, Gaddis, wrote that the Cold War grew mostly out of Soviet expansion, that Stalin pushed and the West pushed back. The other, a revisionist whose name Jessica kept forgetting to write down, argued that American power had provoked the conflict as much as any Russian ambition did, that the United States needed markets and made enemies where it might have made partners. Ms. Zhang had refused to tell the class which one was right. "The evidence," she had said, "does not line up behind a single door. Your job is to weigh, not to pick a side and decorate it."

"You look like you're mad at the books," Isaiah said, dropping into the chair across from her with his own stack, all of it for the same essay. He turned one of her volumes around and scanned the page she'd flagged with a sticky note. She watched his eyes move the way they did when he was actually reading rather than performing it, and she felt briefly less alone in the problem.

"I keep finding that each of them sounds completely convincing until I read the other one," she said. "Gaddis makes the Soviets look like the aggressor, and then the next chapter has the Americans announcing their whole doctrine to Congress like they're proud of it. It's like two lawyers with the same discovery file." She had liked that comparison when it occurred to her on the bus, the idea that history was a trial where the evidence had to be cross-examined before anyone deserved an acquittal.

Ayva came over from the biography aisle holding a thick book with a black and white photograph on the cover. "Okay, so I found the speech everyone quotes," she said, pulling out a chair. "You know how the guide at the memorial last week kept going on about it? He made it sound like Churchill stood up somewhere in Europe and just declared the continent split in half." She flipped to the page she'd marked with a receipt. "But look where it actually happened. Fulton, Missouri. March 5, 1946." She read a few lines aloud, her voice dropping into a faint, borrowed gravitas. "From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent."

"Wait," Isaiah said. "Missouri? He said that in Missouri?" He leaned over the table as though the book might physically extrude the answer, and Jessica noticed something small and strange assembling in her mind, the way a paragraph she'd already read twice suddenly meant something different. Churchill had not been standing behind that curtain when he named it. He had been standing in the middle of the United States, at a small college in the middle of the country, telling Americans what Europe had become. She hadn't thought about where a speech happens before, only what it said.

"That matters," she said slowly, writing it down. "Missouri, March 1946. It's barely a year after the war ended, and he's already describing Europe as divided in two. So both historians can use this same moment and make it say opposite things." She pulled the Gaddis book back toward her. "If you think the Soviets closed the curtain, then Churchill is a witness, an early one, telling the truth before anyone else would. But if you think the West drew the line first, then the speech isn't a description at all, it's a move. It's a man standing in America telling Americans there's an enemy, three years before NATO exists."

Ms. Zhang passed their table on her way to the reference desk and paused, clocking the spread of books, the receipt marking the speech, Isaiah hovering. "You've found the Fulton address," she said, not a question. "It's a good one to sit with." She didn't say anything further, just tapped the cover once and kept walking, and Jessica was oddly grateful for it, the way you're grateful when someone lets you finish a thought you haven't finished yet.

Ayva was less sanguine about the whole project. "So which is it, then?" she asked. "Who started it?" She wanted verdicts; she wanted history to behave like a math problem with a circled answer at the end. Jessica looked at the speech, at the two books, at her notes, which now had a question mark in the margin where a conclusion was supposed to go. The evidence didn't acquit either country, and it didn't convict only one of them, and she was beginning to suspect that the honest essay was the one that said so out loud.

"Maybe the answer is that the curtain was real either way," Jessica said, "and the question is who had an interest in naming it first." She squared her notes, wrote Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946 at the top of a fresh page, and underlined the date twice. "Pass me that other book," she said. "I want to see what he was doing the month before."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
story:
The robotics club kept its member list in a battered blue binder, and by October the binder had one hundred and six names in it, which was why Ms. Dela Cruz gave them fifteen minutes at the start of Tuesday's meeting to find out who had actually paid their dues. "Check each name against the ledger," she said, "before you touch a single motor." Beckham went first, flipping from page one, running his finger down every line while Ana timed him with theatrical cruelty. Six minutes and forty seconds, and he'd found only the names through F. Ana then took over, starting from the back, which she insisted was a superior strategy because "the deadbeats are always the people who joined last." Alexia watched them and felt the particular itch of knowing there was a better way and not yet knowing what it was.

She'd been carrying the library's copy of an algorithms book in her backpack for two weeks, reading it on the bus in guilty fifteen-minute installments the way other people read things they weren't supposed to. Chapter Three had a diagram she'd traced onto her hand during precalculus: a list, a midpoint, a line slicing the page in half. She understood the shape of it but not the mechanics, the way she understood the shape of a college campus from the brochures stacking up in her guidance counselor's office.

"Give me the binder," she said. "And the list of who's paid."

"You don't get to be in charge," Ana said, but she slid the binder across the table anyway.

Alexia found herself at the whiteboard before she'd decided to stand up. "Okay. Say the names were in order. Alphabetical. A hundred and six names. I open to the middle." She tapped a spot in the air. "Say the middle name is Moreno. If the name I want comes before Moreno, alphabetically, then everything after Moreno, the whole second half, is useless to me. It can't be in there. I just throw it away." She drew a stroke through an invisible half of the board. "Then the half that's left, I take its middle, and I do it again."

"Throw away half the list," Beckham said. "Every time."

"That's the part I'm still working on," Alexia said. "Why it's allowed. Why throwing half away isn't cheating."

"Because the list is sorted," Ana said, in the tone of someone explaining that water is wet. Then she paused. "Wait. Is our list sorted?"

Beckham went very still. He turned to the binder, flipped to a random page, and found Nguyen wedged between Cortez and Diaz. Nobody said anything for a second. Then Ana laughed so hard she knocked over the cup of screws.

The plan fell apart and reassembled within the hour. Ms. Dela Cruz offered them the choice of sorting the binder by hand or running a search that actually matched the data they had, and Beckham, who had spent six minutes and forty seconds losing his afternoon to the unsorted version, volunteered to alphabetize all one hundred and six names with a violence that suggested each index card had personally wronged him. Alexia stayed after to help, or to supervise, or possibly just to sit near the problem until it confessed.

Later, walking home, she kept testing the idea against her own skepticism, because her father had raised her on the platitude that if something sounds too good to be true, it is, and halving a hundred things into fifty and fifty into twenty-five sounded exactly that good. But the trick didn't predicate anything on luck or on the good behavior of the data. It demanded one honest thing, sortedness, and one decisive act, throwing away the half that couldn't hold the answer, and then it demanded you trust that act. Flipping page by page through the binder, the way Beckham had, treated every name as equally likely to be anywhere. That was the equivocal position, respectful of all possibilities and loyal to none. The other way took a side. It said: this answer is not in that half, and I'm not looking there.

She tried to explain it to Beckham the next morning before first period, and the telling was where it got hard. "It's not just that it's faster," she said, holding two halves of a torn worksheet. "It's faster because of the order. If the list weren't sorted, the middle name would tell me nothing. Moreno in the middle doesn't mean anything unless everything before it actually comes before it." He nodded slowly, the nod of someone who half had it, and she realized she half had it too, that she could make the machine halve a list all day and still not be sure she could say why in a sentence that would survive a stranger's questions.

At Thursday's meeting they ran it for real. Sorted binder, dues list, Beckham calling out names, Alexia opening to the middle each time, comparing, cutting. Ana, who had bet a granola bar that it wouldn't beat her back-to-front method, watched the finds land in three and four checks apiece and slid the granola bar across the table with the face of a woman paying a debt to history. Ms. Dela Cruz stood at the door with her coffee and said nothing, which was her way of approving.

"Again," Ana said, flipping the binder shut and shuffling the cards like a magician. "And this time I sort them."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
Taylor spread her geography homework across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled of tea and the radiator's dusty heat. The assignment was due Monday: choose a country, analyse its population pyramid, and predict whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes in twenty years. Her grandmother set a mug down beside the laptop and looked over her shoulder at the chart on the screen, two stacked columns of horizontal bars narrowing toward the bottom.

"That's us," her grandmother said, tapping the screen with a bent finger. "Our whole country, in a picture." The bars at the base, the youngest ages, were thinner than the fat middle where her grandmother's own generation sat, and Taylor noticed the shape for the first time, really noticed it. She had skimmed the diagram a dozen times for other assignments without once thinking about what the narrowing meant.

"Can I use this?" she asked, mostly to herself, and pulled the chart closer. The base narrower than the middle. She copied the outline onto a napkin with a pencil, and her grandmother watched her draw as though she were mapping weather. "Fewer kids than there are people my age," her grandmother said. "I could have told them that. There were forty in my class and eight in your mother's."

Taylor's phone buzzed. Reuben had sent a photo of his own pyramid, Japan's, with the caption "this one looks like an upside down tree, what do i even write." She typed back that she hadn't figured it out yet, which was true, and then sat with the napkin. If the base was narrower, birth rates were falling, and the fat middle would keep moving upward into old age. She wrote at the bottom of her page: nursing homes, not schools. Then she crossed it out, because crossing things out felt like thinking, and wrote it again.

Her grandmother had gone to the counter to cut bread, moving carefully, one hand on her hip. Taylor watched her and felt the assignment shift under her, the way a lake shifts when you realize how deep it goes. "Grandma," she said, "who's going to work at those nursing homes? In twenty years, I mean. If there are more old people and fewer young ones." The question had not been on the sheet Mr. Sok handed out, but once she had asked it aloud she could not unask it.

Her grandmother laughed, a short sound. "You'll be working at one, dear, changing my hypothetical sheets." But Taylor kept looking at the chart, at the middle bars inching toward the top of the graph where the numbers thinned to nothing. "I'm being serious. It's the actual question. The pyramid says one thing, care, homes, all of it, but it doesn't say who does the caring." Her grandmother was quiet then, slicing the bread evenly, and the kitchen held only the knife's small rhythm.

Taylor opened a new document and typed two paragraphs. In the first she laid out the shape as evidence: a base narrower than its middle meant falling birth rates and an aging population, which pointed to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care rather than schools. She let that stand clean and definite, because the data was definite. In the second paragraph she wrote about the uncertainty the data could not circumscribe, the question of staffing, of migration, of whether young people like her would stay in the country at all. She was honest in that paragraph, perhaps more honest than Mr. Sok wanted, writing that she could predict the buildings a country would need but not the hands that would fill them. Entropy, she typed, then deleted, then typed again in a smaller sentence: the chart showed a kind of entropy, a system running down toward fewer, older lives, and no pyramid could show you the push against it.

Reuben texted again. "maddox says just write 'old people' and move on." Taylor smiled at the screen, aware that Maddox's answer was the mercurial one, easy today, gone tomorrow, and that her own answer would cost her something to defend in class. She wrote back, "I'm writing that we'll need the homes. And then I'm writing the question about who staffs them. He can mark it however he wants."

Her grandmother brought two plates of bread and cheese to the table and sat down across from the napkin drawing, turning it to face herself. She studied the narrowing base the way one studies a face, and Taylor watched her look at her own generation bulging in the middle of the page. "You know," her grandmother said, "when I was your age, I thought the hardest thing would be having children. Turns out the hard part is everything after." She slid the napkin back across the table, and Taylor tucked it into her binder, between the pages, evidence.

story:
Clara had been drawing the school hallway for two days and it refused to become a hallway. On paper it was a corridor the way a diagram of a whale is a whale: doors in a row, lockers in a row, floor tiles like graph paper, everything obedient and dead flat. She sat at the long table by the window in Mr. Morales's art classroom, third period, pressing her pencil harder as if pressure could push the drawing backward into space.

"You're poking at it," Halle said from across the table, not looking up from her clay coil pot. "You do that when you're stuck. It's a mannerism, like my mom checking the stove three times." Clara looked down and realized her pencil was indeed jabbing the paper in small irritated strokes, so she set it on the table and put both hands in her lap.

The assignment was simple, which was the problem. Mr. Morales had asked for a drawing of a place you walk through every day, due Friday, and he had said almost nothing else, which was either laziness or something munificent Clara hadn't figured out yet, a gift of silence she didn't know how to spend. Other kids had chosen their bedrooms, the bus stop, the gym. Clara had chosen the east hallway because she had art in this room and chemistry at the far end of it, and she had walked it maybe four hundred times without once looking at it.

She did look now, or tried to. What made a hallway a hallway, when you stood in one? The walls were parallel. The floor was parallel to the ceiling. But when she held up her pencil at arm's length and sighted along the wall, squinting one eye, the baseboard line ran downhill toward the far door, and the top of the lockers ran downhill too, the two lines leaning toward each other like people sharing an umbrella. Her drawing had them parallel and level. That was the flatness. That was the corpse of the hallway lying on the page.

Domenico slid into the seat beside her, late as always, smelling of the parking lot. He looked at her drawing for a long, theatrical moment. "That's a hallway for ants," he said. "A flat hallway. A hallway drawn by someone who has never been in a hallway."

"Thank you, Domenico."

"I mean it as a diagnosis." He leaned over her shoulder. "Where's the vanishing point?"

She stared at him. "The what?"

"The vanishing point. Where all the lines run together and disappear." He took a scrap paper and sketched a fast box of a street, the building edges all sliding toward a single dot near the middle, and suddenly the scrap had depth, suddenly you could walk into it. "Some Renaissance guy did this," he said. "Filippo Brunelleschi. Around 1420, in Florence. He demonstrated it to everybody, linear perspective, drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point so a flat surface shows depth. Mr. Morales went on about him last year when I had him for studio. I mostly remembered the dot."

Clara took the scrap and held it beside her drawing. Her hallway had no dot. It had no place where anything ran together. It had four hundred walks' worth of nothing.

That night she wrote to her brother, who was doing a design degree two states away and answered faster when she claimed to be desperate. She texted: "Is it cheating if I mark a point on my paper and make every line in the hallway aim at it? It feels like cheating. Like the hallway isn't really like that, the lines aren't really converging, the walls are parallel, I measured." His reply came while she was eating cereal: "They're parallel in the world. They converge in your eye. The drawing is a picture of your eye, not of the world. Also it's not cheating, it's five hundred years old." She read it four times, then folded it into a wondering question she carried to sleep: if the drawing was a picture of her eye, then every drawing anyone had ever made was secretly a self-portrait of looking.

The next morning she did not draw the hallway. She drew a dot. She put it in the center of the page, lightly, apologetically, like a trespasser marking a claim. Then she ruled lines from the dot outward: floor, ceiling, both baseboards, the top edges of the lockers, the lintels of the doors marching away. She worked the doors in one at a time, each smaller and higher in the picture than the last, each fitting between the converging lines like beads on a string. When she placed the floor tiles she stopped drawing squares and drew receding lines toward the dot crossed by slowly flattening horizontals, and the tiles tipped away from her, row after row, and her stomach did something odd, as though she were actually standing there, actually walking in.

Halle came over with wet clay hands held away from her body. She looked a long time without speaking. "It's deep," she said finally, with some surprise, as if Clara had performed a surgery.

"It's borrowed," Clara said. "It's a trick from 1420. I don't fully get whether it's the truth about hallways or a lie we all agreed to believe." She wasn't sure, and she said so, and found that saying it didn't spoil the drawing. Domenico was right about the dot. Her brother was right about the eye. Somewhere between the two, the hallway existed, and she had put it on paper, and both things could be true, the parallel walls and the converging lines, and she could hold them without either one calcifying into a rule.

Mr. Morales walked the room slowly during the last fifteen minutes. When he reached her table he stopped, tilted his head, and looked down the drawing like a man sighting along a wall.

"Stand here a second," he said. "Where's the dot?"

She touched the pencil mark, still faint, at the center of the corridor. "Right there."

He nodded once. "Keep it visible."

"Visible? I was going to erase it."

"Don't." He moved on down the row of tables, and Clara leaned close, shading a tile, the lines running away from her toward the small gray point where everything met.
